title: Budget Cuts Develop Ulcers, Not Products

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I cut your product development budget by 25%, what could you develop?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ulcers, heart disease and maybe mysterious pustules.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How about the product itself?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It will envy me.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is going to cut the product development budget by 25% and asks what Dilbert could still develop. Dilbert, seated at his computer, answers that he would develop health problems. When the Boss asks about the product itself, Dilbert says the product will envy him.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that the stress of a slashed budget will leave him sick and the product so badly done that it would be better off in his miserable shape.
summary: Told his funding is being slashed, an engineer sarcastically predicts that the only things growing will be his illnesses, while the product itself will end up in worse shape.

title: Boss Steals Idea Repeated Back

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I recommend that we eliminate the least popular features because they cost us more than they generate in revenue.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have an idea. Let's eliminate the least popular features to save money.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I suggest that we eliminate the least popular features.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I steal that idea to infinity.

situation: Dilbert proposes cutting the least popular product features because they cost more than they earn. The Boss responds as if he has just had the same idea himself, taking credit for it. When Dilbert repeats the suggestion, the Boss declares that he steals the idea 'to infinity', as though claiming it forever.
punchline: The Boss shamelessly claims credit for Dilbert's idea, and even a repeat of the suggestion can't win it back because he steals it 'to infinity', a childish trump card.
summary: A manager passes off an employee's cost-cutting suggestion as his own and then uses a playground-style comeback to keep ownership of it.

title: Feng Shui Customer Called Witch Doctor

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Visiting a customer

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Our office was designed with the science of feng shui.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I describe the technical merits of our product or will you be consulting with a witch doctor?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oops. Sorry. That one snuck up on me.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: He's an astrologer, not a witch doctor.

situation: Dilbert visits a customer who proudly says his office was designed using feng shui. Dilbert sarcastically asks whether he should explain his product's technical merits or whether the customer will consult a witch doctor instead. After apologizing for the slip, the customer corrects him that his adviser is an astrologer, not a witch doctor.
punchline: Dilbert's insult is not defused by his apology, because the customer only quibbles over which type of pseudoscience adviser he uses, confirming he does make decisions based on superstition.
summary: A salesman's snide remark about superstitious decision-making gets a deadpan correction about the exact flavor of mysticism involved.

file: 2004/2004-04-25_international pop star_downloaded cd_burned guitar_poor_made no money_manager stole.gif
title: Pop Star Who Sold Zero CDs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your last job was ...international pop star?

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, I recognize you! I bought your new CD!

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: No you didn't.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When I say "bought," I mean downloaded.

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: Exactly. I didn't sell one CD. Everyone downloaded it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Weren't you already rich?

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: My business manager stole everything.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You could perform live.

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: Too many musicians, not enough venues.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now do you make music for the love of it?

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: I burned my guitar for heat.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I bought your new CD!

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: No you didn't.

setting: A job interview in the boss's office, with a final panel in a cubicle area
situation: The Boss interviews a pink-haired applicant who claims to have been an international pop star. The boss says he bought the applicant's CD, but it turns out he only downloaded it, which is why the star made no money. The star explains that a business manager stole his earnings, live gigs are impossible, and he burned his guitar for heat, and in the last panel another employee makes the same false claim.
punchline: The pop star is so broke from music piracy and theft that he burned his guitar for heat, and everyone keeps claiming to have bought a CD they actually downloaded for free.
summary: A once-famous musician applying for a job reveals that file sharing and a thieving manager left him destitute, while everyone he meets insists they bought his album.

title: Dogbert Leases His Own Advice

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You should offer your customers easy financing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That disguises the true cost of your products so you can price-gouge and people will thank you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How much are we paying you?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm leasing my advice to you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thank you!

setting: Conference room during a consulting session
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises a manager to offer easy financing so customers can't see the true cost of the products and can be price-gouged. When the Boss asks what the advice will cost, Dogbert says he is leasing it, so the Boss never sees the real price. The Boss thanks him, falling for the exact trick Dogbert just described.
punchline: Dogbert demonstrates his own price-obscuring financing scheme on the Boss, who gratefully accepts being fleeced without even knowing the real cost.
summary: A consultant dog pitches a trick for hiding true prices, then uses it on his gullible client right away.

file: 2004/2004-01-06_cell phone bill_expense_award_speech_lost cell phone_low bill_company phone.gif
title: Wally Rewarded for Losing Phone

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The Expense Cutters Award goes to Wally for drastically lowering his cell phone bill.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, would you like to say a few words to the group?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I lost my phone last month. Hey, thanks for the hundred dollars!

setting: Conference room during an awards meeting
situation: The Boss presents the Expense Cutters Award to Wally for drastically reducing his cell phone bill and invites him to give a speech. Wally stands up, admits he simply lost his phone, and happily counts the hundred-dollar prize money while Dilbert and a coworker look on.
punchline: Wally's cost savings came from losing his phone rather than any real effort, yet he gets rewarded with cash for it, exposing how management rewards accidental results.
summary: A manager hands out a cost-cutting prize to Wally, who cheerfully reveals his savings were just the result of misplacing his phone.

title: Wireless Hassock-Buddy Stalks Its Owner

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I finished the prototype for the wireless hassock-buddy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It uses GPS navigation to stalk its owner and demand that he rest his feet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Today I learned to avoid the words "stalk" and "aaagh" in my PowerPoint presentations.

setting: Conference room with a projected presentation slide
situation: Dilbert presents a prototype for a wireless hassock-buddy, a footstool that uses GPS to follow its owner around. The slide shows a stick figure screaming in terror as the device chases him. In the last panel Dilbert reflects on the poor choice of words while Dogbert sits nearby.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to pitch a helpful gadget accidentally describes and illustrates something so creepy and menacing that the presentation backfires, and his lesson is merely about word choice rather than the product being bad.
summary: An engineer pitches a footstool that tracks down its owner by GPS, only to realize his slides make it sound like a horror movie.

file: 2004/2004-02-04_new chip_slower_claim fastest_benchmark test_used old drivers_wearing a wire_marketing_crime_business.gif
title: Marketing Fastest Claim for Slower Chip

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our new chip is slower than our competition's products.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll claim we're the fastest. If anyone does benchmark tests, we'll say they used old drivers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whenever I talk to you, I feel like I should be wearing a wire.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Since when is marketing a crime?

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that the company's new chip is slower than the competition's products. The Boss plans to claim it is the fastest anyway and to blame old drivers if anyone runs benchmark tests. Dilbert says he feels like he should be wearing a wire, and the Boss asks since when marketing is a crime.
punchline: The Boss's plan to make false performance claims is clearly deceptive, yet he genuinely sees it as ordinary marketing, implying that lying is simply standard practice in the field.
summary: A boss cheerfully plans to advertise a sluggish processor as the quickest on the market and dismisses an engineer's ethical unease as an overreaction.

title: Typo Reveals Market of One

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I discovered a typo in the market forecast that is driving our company strategy.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Where it says, "Everyone would want one," it should have said, "Avery Wong would want one."

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Worse yet, I called Mr. Wong and he said he was joking.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What if we gave him free delivery?

situation: An employee reports to the boss that a typo in the market forecast, which is the basis of the company's strategy, changed the meaning from universal demand to demand from a single person named Avery Wong. He adds that Mr. Wong said he was only joking when contacted. The boss responds by suggesting they offer Mr. Wong free delivery.
punchline: The boss ignores the collapse of the entire strategy's premise and instead tries to salvage it by courting the one customer who supposedly wants the product.
summary: A whole company strategy turns out to rest on a single misprinted word, and the boss's fix is to bribe the lone would-be customer.

file: 2004/2004-02-02_porject_top prioroty_tell everything_bored_can't stay awake_haven't talked yet_gets worse.gif
title: Boss Bored Before Dilbert Speaks

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your project is my top priority. Tell me everything that I need to know.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm so bored... Can't... Stay... Awake.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I haven't started talking yet.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It gets worse??!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: O-o-okay

setting: Conference room or meeting table in the office
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert his project is a top priority and asks to be told everything he needs to know. Before Dilbert has said a single word, the Boss is already slumped back in his chair, falling asleep from boredom. When Dilbert points out he hasn't started yet, the Boss is horrified that it will get worse, and Dilbert nervously agrees to proceed.
punchline: The Boss claims the project is his top priority, yet he is bored to the point of sleep just anticipating the explanation, showing his stated priorities are empty words.
summary: A manager who swears a project is vital nearly dozes off before the engineer even begins his briefing.

file: 2004/2004-02-26_dance with death_secreatry_desk_work to early grave_first to drop_good morning_first thing_competition_resentment_anger.gif
title: Alice and Boss's Deadly Rivalry

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Well, look who came back to dance with death.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Once again you will try to work me to an early grave and I will book you on dangerous business trips.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Who will be the first to drop? Who?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What ever happened to "good morning"?

situation: The Boss arrives at work carrying his briefcase, and Alice greets him with open hostility at her desk. She declares an ongoing contest in which he overworks her while she retaliates by booking him on dangerous business trips. She asks who will die first, and the Boss can only ask why she doesn't just say good morning.
punchline: Alice and the Boss are locked in a mutual, lethal grudge match, and the Boss's mild request for a polite greeting shows how absurdly far the hostility has escalated.
summary: A hostile employee greets her manager with a grim promise of mutual destruction, leaving him wishing for a simple hello.

file: 2004/2004-01-17_concierge_hotel_slave_do naything_oo much_donate kidney_kiss up_over trained_give pay.gif
title: Hotel Clerk Over-Trained In Service

transcript.speaker: Hotel Clerk
transcript.text: Welcome to the Metrogarden Hotel! How may I make your stay incredible?

transcript.speaker: Hotel Clerk
transcript.text: I would be delighted to iron your socks, examine you for suspicious moles or take a second job and give you my pay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think they over-trained you.

transcript.speaker: Hotel Clerk
transcript.text: I'm shaved and prepped to donate a kidney.

situation: Dilbert arrives with his luggage at the Metrogarden Hotel front desk. The clerk greets him and offers increasingly absurd services, such as ironing his socks, checking him for moles and giving him a second job's pay. Dilbert remarks that the clerk was over-trained, and the clerk responds that he is already prepped to donate a kidney.
punchline: The clerk's customer-service training has pushed him into absurd, self-sacrificing servility, culminating in his readiness to donate an organ to a guest.
summary: A hotel employee's zeal to please a guest escalates from sock-pressing to offering a kidney, showing how far service-culture training can go.

file: 2004/2004-02-27_paranoid_emplooyees_trying to kill_pauses between words_no payment_ruled out paranoia_session_therapist session_crazy_couch_offensive_cheap_reluctance to heal.gif
title: Boss Is Not Paranoid, Therapist Rules

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think my employees are trying to kill me. Am I paranoid?

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: Put your answer in an e-mail. I don't want to be paying for the pauses between your words.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: I've ruled out paranoia.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Phew! That's a relief.

situation: The Boss lies on a therapy couch and asks his therapist whether he is paranoid for believing his employees are trying to kill him. The therapist, who is oddly concerned about the time she is billed for, tells him to email his answer instead of speaking slowly. She then announces she has ruled out paranoia, which reassures him.
punchline: The therapist's conclusion that he isn't paranoid means his employees really are trying to kill him, yet the oblivious Boss is relieved.
summary: A manager frets on a therapist's couch about a murder plot by his staff and is cheerfully reassured when the doctor says it is not paranoia.

file: 2004/2004-01-01_office relocation_procedures_wrong cubicle_easily stealable_move computer_rules and regulations_company rules.gif
title: Office Move Rules Are Absurd

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Office relocation

transcript.speaker: Facilities Employee
transcript.text: You are not allowed to move your own computer.

transcript.speaker: Facilities Employee
transcript.text: It must be left in an easily stealable condition for three days until the movers take it to the wrong cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Facilities Employee
transcript.text: Then untrained I.T. professionals will shove an ethernet cable into your stapler and call it good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Get out of my way.

setting: Office hallway during an office relocation
situation: A facilities employee holding a clipboard explains the company's relocation rules to Dilbert, who is carrying his own computer equipment. The rules forbid moving your own computer and describe a chaotic process of theft risk, misdelivery and botched reconnection by untrained IT staff. Dilbert ignores the rules and pushes past him.
punchline: The official relocation procedure is so inept that Dilbert would rather break the rules and move his own computer than trust the process.
summary: A clipboard-wielding functionary lays out an office move policy so ridiculous that its target simply shoulders past him with his own gear.

file: 2004/2004-02-23_competitors_tired_unfocused_pester_endless series_charity request_employee birthday parties_blood drives_can't focus.gif
title: Dogbert Exhausts Competitors With Distractions

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can make your competitors tired and unfocused.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll pester them with an endless series of charity requests, employee birthday parties and blood drives.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I know it works because they paid me to do it to you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... tired. Can't... focus.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, pitches the Boss on a plan to sabotage his competitors by burying them in charity requests, birthday parties and blood drives. He then reveals that the Boss's own competitors hired him to do exactly that to the Boss, and the Boss is visibly worn out and unable to concentrate.
punchline: Dogbert proves his method works by exhausting the Boss himself, since the Boss's competitors are the ones paying him to do it.
summary: A scheming consultant demonstrates his distraction tactics on the very client he is pitching, who is already too drained to react.

title: Dogbert's Incompetent Composite Logo

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your company has become synonymous with incompetence and crime.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Stop trying to be all things to all people. Focus on either the incompetence or the crime.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For your new logo, I used computer graphics to create a composite face that looks totally incompetent.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow.

situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant, tells a company's executives that their business is known for both incompetence and crime. He advises them to pick one and then shows a new logo: a computer-generated composite face that looks totally incompetent. The Boss is impressed by it.
punchline: Dogbert's branding advice is to commit to one reputation, and the logo he designs looks so incompetent that the company chose incompetence on purpose.
summary: A consulting dog tells a shady company to specialize in either bumbling or lawbreaking, then unveils a logo that makes the choice unmistakable.

title: Business Travel Approval Misery List

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need your approval to...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...be exhausted, bored, stiff, head-achey, annoyed and constipated for the next three days.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Also known as "business travel."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I must be traveling right now!

situation: Dilbert stands at the Boss's desk asking for approval, then lists a string of miserable symptoms he wants permission to suffer. He reveals that this list is simply what business travel feels like. The Boss responds that he must be traveling right now, implying his own job leaves him feeling the same.
punchline: The Boss unwittingly admits that his everyday office life feels as miserable as being on a business trip.
summary: An employee requests permission to endure a list of physical and mental discomforts, which turns out to be a description of work travel, and his boss claims to be experiencing the same thing at his desk.

file: 2004/2004-01-08_involuntary sepration_payroll_fired_can't touch anything_way of saying fired.gif
title: Fired Via Euphemistic Payroll Separation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, you're going to experience an involuntary separation from payroll.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I'm fired.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No-o-o-o. It's just that you won't be part of the payroll system.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you're not allowed to touch anything.

setting: Boss's office, seated across a desk
situation: The Boss tells Ted he will undergo an 'involuntary separation from payroll.' Ted correctly translates this as being fired, and the Boss denies it, only rephrasing the same news in slightly different words. He then adds that Ted can't touch anything, which is a standard part of being fired.
punchline: The Boss insists Ted isn't fired, yet every detail he adds, being removed from payroll and forbidden to touch anything, describes exactly what being fired means.
summary: A manager tries to dodge the word 'fired' with corporate jargon, but his own clarifications confirm the termination.

file: 2004/2004-03-03_ytransferred_new job_secretary job eliminated_masive incompetence_resentment_anger_splitting mad_offers new job.gif
title: Fired Then Hired as Secretary

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, two things: First, I got transferred to a new job, and that means your job here is eliminated.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Why must I suffer for your massive incompetence? You worthless pile of stinkin' crud!!!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: And the second thing?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll need a secretary at the new job.

situation: The Boss tells his secretary Carol that he has been transferred and her job is being eliminated. Carol explodes in anger, blaming his incompetence and insulting him. She then calmly asks about the second thing, and he says he needs a secretary at his new job.
punchline: After being told she is laid off because of his incompetence, Carol learns the second thing is that he wants her to be his secretary again, so her outburst was in vain.
summary: A manager's reassignment costs his assistant her position, but he promptly offers her a job working for him in the new role.

file: 2004/2004-01-03_office relocation._new cubicle_less roomy_need butter_torso_slide in_attracts rats_cheap_low budget.gif
title: Butter Required for Tiny Cubicle

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Office relocation

transcript.speaker: Facilities Employee
transcript.text: Your new cubicle is less roomy than the old one. You will need this butter.

transcript.speaker: Facilities Employee
transcript.text: Apply it liberally to your torso area and you can slide right in.

transcript.speaker: Facilities Employee
transcript.text: But don't stay in there for more than 10 minutes at a time because it attracts rats.

setting: Office hallway during an office relocation
situation: A facilities employee holding a clipboard tells Alice that her new cubicle is smaller than her old one and hands her a stick of butter. He instructs her to rub it on her torso so she can squeeze in, then warns her not to stay inside for more than 10 minutes because the butter attracts rats. Alice looks increasingly unimpressed.
punchline: The company solves its shrinking cubicle space with a ridiculous, unsanitary fix, and the fix itself creates a new problem: rats.
summary: A relocation worker gives a colleague butter to squeeze into a cramped new workspace, then casually mentions the vermin risk it creates.

file: 2004/2004-03-05_new boss_goat head_puts spell_workers_finish project_sadistic_fair_witch as boss_motivation.gif
title: Witch Boss Curses Slackers Motivationally

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The new boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you'll be more motivated with a goat head.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The spell won't go away until you finish your project.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: She's a big improvement over our last boss.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: She's sadistic but she's fair.

situation: The new boss, a witch in a pointed hat, waves her wand and turns an employee's head into a goat head as punishment for not finishing her project. The spell stays until the work is done. Two coworkers holding coffee mugs, one of them already transformed into a rodent-like creature, say the witch is better than the previous boss.
punchline: The workers consider a boss who magically curses them to be an improvement, because she is at least sadistic but fair, implying the previous boss was worse.
summary: A spell-casting witch manager transforms a lagging employee's head to force productivity, and her staff cheerfully call her an upgrade.

title: Smokers Powering Computers With Seesaw

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The smokers in this building take hundreds of trips outside to smoke every day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We can harness that kinetic energy to create electricity to power their unused computers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Too much slope.

transcript.speaker: Smoker
transcript.text: Pant pant

setting: Office presentation area and a test site with a makeshift seesaw
situation: Dilbert presents an idea to harness the energy smokers expend walking outside to smoke, using it to generate electricity for their idle computers. His diagram shows a seesaw-like generator. In the last panel he tests it with a real smoker, who is exhausted and gasping on a steeply tilted ramp while Dilbert takes notes on a clipboard.
punchline: Dilbert treats the winded, exhausted smoker as a mere engineering problem, concluding only that the slope is too steep, with no concern for the person being used as a power source.
summary: An engineer's plan to turn smokers' exertion into electricity ends with a gasping test subject and a clinical complaint about the incline.

title: Boss Power Shops Employee's Computer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's time to go power shopping.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nice computer. Did you just get it?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Shopping always puts me in a good mood.

setting: Office cubicle area and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss, seated at his desk, decides he wants to go power shopping. He walks up to an employee, compliments the new computer, and the employee cries out in alarm. In the last panel the Boss walks off carrying the employee's computer, its cables still dragging the distressed employee behind him.
punchline: The Boss's idea of 'shopping' is simply taking a computer from a subordinate without paying or asking, and he is cheerfully oblivious to the theft.
summary: A manager treats walking off with a coworker's brand-new machine as a pleasant shopping trip.

title: Sleeping Passenger Pins Dilbert's Hands

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Six-hour flight; I can get lots of work done.

transcript.speaker: Passenger
transcript.text: Six-hour flight; I can get lots of sleep.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't feel my hands!!!

setting: Airplane cabin during a six-hour flight
situation: Dilbert settles into his airplane seat planning to work on his laptop for the whole flight. The man seated in front of him has the opposite plan and intends to sleep. In the last panel the passenger has reclined his seat or slumped back so far that Dilbert's hands are trapped beneath it.
punchline: Both passengers plan to use the same long flight in incompatible ways, and the sleeper's reclined seat crushes Dilbert's hands and his hopes of working.
summary: Two travelers make conflicting plans for a long flight, and the one in front wins by flattening the one behind.

title: Boss Reorganizes Out of Boredom

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's been a few hours since I've done anything managerish.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I could criticize someone...nah. I could have a meeting...nah.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm reorganizing the department!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Excuse me while I beat myself with my keyboard.

setting: The Boss's office and Dilbert's cubicle
situation: The Boss sits idly at his desk, thinking that it has been hours since he did anything managerial. After dismissing criticizing someone or holding a meeting, he settles on reorganizing the department and announces it to Dilbert. Dilbert reacts by saying he will beat himself with his keyboard.
punchline: The Boss reorganizes the department purely to relieve his own boredom, and Dilbert's sarcastic reaction shows how much damage and misery reorganizations cause employees.
summary: Restless from a lack of managerial activity, a boss picks a sweeping reshuffle as his next pastime, prompting an employee to prefer self-inflicted pain.

title: Dogbert's Sycophant School Head-Nodding Lesson

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Welcome to Dogbert's School for Worthless Sycophants.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our first lesson is "Head Nodding for Beginners."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Good, good... Now get ready to snap it forward.

situation: Dogbert, acting as headmaster, welcomes a class of adults to his school for worthless sycophants and begins the first lesson on head nodding. In the last panel the students are all tilting their heads far back in unison, and Dogbert instructs them to snap their heads forward.
punchline: Sycophantic agreement is treated as a trainable, mechanical skill, so the students must rehearse a perfectly timed, synchronized nod to look convincingly eager to agree.
summary: A canine instructor drills his pupils in the art of choreographed, enthusiastic nodding so they can flatter their superiors on cue.

file: 2004/2004-01-29_safety law_ceo_email ceo_blah blah blah_negligence_people die_products safety.gif
title: CEO Ignores Deadly Safety Warning

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you refuse to do something about our product's safety flaw, I will be forced to contact our CEO!

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Try it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This e-mail will make him drop everything and call me.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Hundreds will die... blah, blah, blah... whatever. Forward the message to that Pointy-Haired guy.

situation: Dilbert threatens an executive that he will go to the CEO if the company doesn't fix a product safety flaw. The executive dares him to try, so Dilbert emails the CEO, confident it will provoke an immediate call. The CEO skims the warning about hundreds of deaths, dismisses it, and tells his assistant to forward it to the Pointy-Haired Boss.
punchline: The CEO is so indifferent to a life-threatening safety flaw that he brushes off the warning and passes it to the least competent manager, so the problem will never be fixed.
summary: An engineer's escalation of a deadly product defect reaches the top, only to be waved off and handed to the company's most useless manager.

title: Paper Prop for Looking Busy

transcript.text: Now when I wander the hallways looking busy I can totally rest my hand.

transcript.speaker: Wally

situation: Wally proudly shows a coworker a sheet of paper he has modified with a finger holder, so he can carry it around while appearing busy and still rest his hand. punchline: Wally gives away his ruse by cheerfully admitting he isn't working hard, which defeats the whole purpose of carrying a paper to look busy.
summary: A lazy employee engineers a prop to fake busyness while strolling the corridors, then blows his own cover with a candid reply.

summary: A consultant dog pitches an elite innovation team with every luxury, then casually mentions that everyone left behind gets a once-a-year sightseeing visit.

title: Intern Denied Promotion, Must Train Replacement

transcript.text: I heard that you got approval to hire a new senior engineer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I plan to hire someone from outside the company.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Must...control... ...tiny...fists... of intern fury.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have approval to fill the senior engineer position but there's a ban on hiring new interns.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So if I promote you, my empire...oops... I mean my department won't grow.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! My despair has turned into a searing psychological pain!!!

situation: An intern who says he has done a senior engineer's job for five years asks to be promoted into the open senior position. The Boss refuses and plans to hire an outsider, because promoting the intern would leave him unable to backfill the intern slot and would shrink his department. The intern is crushed, and the Boss adds insult to injury by telling him to train the new hire.
punchline: The Boss denies the intern a well-earned promotion to protect his own headcount, then makes the intern train the outsider who gets the job.
summary: A long-suffering intern is passed over for the senior job he has effectively been doing, only to be told to train his outside replacement.

file: 2004/2004-01-27_deadly safety flaw_stock plunge_massive layoffs_ruined career_dead customers_hardest.gif
title: Hiding Deadly Flaw Protects Stock

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wally, I discovered a deadly safety flaw in our product. Who should I inform?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No one. The stock would plunge and we'd have massive layoffs. Your career would be ruined.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But my negligence could cause the deaths of a dozen customers.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The first dozen is always the hardest.

situation: Asok, holding a paper, tells Wally he has found a deadly safety flaw in the company's product and asks who he should report it to. Wally advises telling no one, since disclosure would crash the stock price, cause layoffs and ruin Asok's career. When Asok worries that customers could die, Wally callously says the first dozen deaths are the hardest to live with.
punchline: Wally treats customer deaths as a minor hurdle that gets easier to ignore with practice, showing how corporate self-preservation can override basic ethics.
summary: A junior employee asks whom to tell about a lethal product defect and gets cynical advice to bury it, with the coworker joking that guilt fades after the first few victims.

title: Morale Improves When Boss Stops Managing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been named the aspect manager of morale. Effective today, you no longer report to me.

transcript.speaker: Employees
transcript.text: Yippeee!!! Woo-hoo!! Yes!!

transcript.speaker: Upper Manager
transcript.text: How did you improve the morale so quickly?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm a genius?

setting: Conference room and an executive's office
situation: The Boss announces to his staff in a meeting that he has been made the manager of morale and that they no longer report to him. The employees erupt in cheers. Later, a senior manager asks how he raised morale so fast, and the Boss takes credit, unaware of the real reason.
punchline: Morale soared only because the staff were overjoyed to be rid of the Boss, yet he sincerely believes his own genius caused it.
summary: A clueless manager claims credit for a morale boom that was really just his team celebrating his departure as their boss.

situation: In a meeting, the Boss admits nobody has sold a single unit of the new wireless hassock and announces a plan to have salespeople work in teams and take turns wearing electroshock pants. In the final panel, one salesman holds a remote control and threatens his shock-wearing teammate Cliffy to close the deal, while Cliffy desperately shouts at a customer to buy it.
punchline: Management's solution to poor sales is to literally torture salespeople with electric shocks, turning sales pressure and teamwork into physical punishment.
summary: A manager's answer to dismal product sales is a team scheme in which salespeople zap each other with shock-delivering trousers until a customer relents.

situation: Dilbert waits in line at airport security as announcements tell passengers what to remove for screening. The requests escalate from jackets and shoes to their skin, and by the last panel the passengers are skeletons carrying their skin in bins, now warned against mentioning infamous box-office flops.
punchline: Airport security rules grow so absurdly intrusive that travelers are stripped down to skeletons and then legally barred from even joking about notorious bad movies.
summary: Ever-escalating airport screening instructions leave travelers as bare skeletons who are then forbidden from naming three famous flop films.

file: 2004/2004-02-13_look like moron_magazine cover_misquote_morning on parade_quotes area ccuarte_writers.gif
title: Boss Relieved By Accurate Quotes

setting: Office, in a cubicle area and then the Boss's own office
situation: A coworker hands the Boss a magazine called "Morons on Parade" and tells him he made the cover. The Boss worries that writers may have misquoted him to make him look foolish, then reads the article in his chair and is relieved that every quote is accurate.
punchline: The Boss is happy that his words were quoted correctly, failing to realize that accurate quotes are exactly what made him look like a moron.
summary: A manager checks a magazine about fools to be sure he wasn't unfairly misrepresented, then celebrates that his own genuine words got him featured.

file: 2004/2004-01-30_deadly product_sued_did nothing_public realtions_goal_jury pool_victims deserved it_moral implications_strategy.gif
title: Dogbert's PR: Blame the Victims

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert does P.R.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You knew your product was deadly but you did nothing until you were sued.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The goal of public relations is to taint the jury pool. We'll show that the victims had it coming.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we should discuss the moral implications of that strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bah!

situation: Dogbert, working as a public relations consultant, meets with Dilbert and The Boss around a conference table. Dilbert points out the company knew its product was deadly and did nothing until sued, and Dogbert explains that PR exists to bias the jury pool by painting the victims as deserving their fate. When Dilbert raises the moral implications, Dogbert dismisses him.
punchline: Dogbert cynically defines public relations as manipulating juries and smearing victims, and waves off ethical concerns with a contemptuous 'Bah!'
summary: A consultant dog cheerfully explains that corporate PR means poisoning public opinion against the people a lethal product harmed, then brushes off an ethics objection.

title: Dogbert Says Customers Lack Credibility

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Never listen to your customers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They were dumb enough to buy your product, so they have no credibility.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That reminds me: Thanks for buying my services. Don't talk. Shhhh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ooh.

setting: Conference room during a consulting session
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises a boss and a female executive to never listen to their customers because anyone who bought their product must be foolish. He then realizes that the same logic applies to his own clients, so he thanks them for buying his services and tells them to be quiet.
punchline: Dogbert's reasoning that customers who buy a product lack credibility also discredits his own clients, so he hastily silences them to protect his consulting fee.
summary: A canine consultant tells his clients that buyers are fools whose opinions are worthless, then notices he just insulted the very people paying him and shushes them.

title: Whistleblower Guilt Meets Alice's Scone

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Alice, if I fail to blow the whistle on our product's safety problem, I will be like a murderer!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: No, technically you'd be more like a killer, you wuss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My guts feel like I swallowed a squirrel.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You have totally sucked the flavor out of this scone.

situation: Dilbert agonizes to Alice about whether to report a safety problem in their product, saying that staying silent would make him like a murderer. Alice, who is eating a scone, coldly corrects his terminology and calls him a wuss. When he says his stomach feels awful, she complains only that his moral dilemma has ruined her snack.
punchline: Alice is so callous that she treats a serious ethical crisis as a mere annoyance to her breakfast, showing more concern for her scone than for potential product-related deaths.
summary: A conscience-stricken coworker frets over reporting a dangerous product defect while his colleague nitpicks his wording and grumbles that his worry is spoiling her pastry.

title: Boss Contradicts Dilbert to Matthew

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He says you have no credibility.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss he has already told a client named Matthew that the requested changes are impossible. The phone rings and the boss cheerfully assures Matthew that the changes can certainly be made. He then hangs up and tells Dilbert that Matthew says Dilbert has no credibility.
punchline: The boss undermines Dilbert by contradicting him to the client and then blames the resulting loss of credibility on Dilbert instead of himself.
summary: A boss overrides his employee's honest answer to a client and then pins the damaged trust on the employee.

punchline: The Boss is so oblivious that he cheerfully approves a ridiculous name that Dogbert openly says advertises his total lack of awareness.
summary: A canine consultant mocks a clueless executive with a silly corporate rebrand, and the executive takes it as a compliment.

situation: Dilbert is packing clothes for a flight while Dogbert sits on the bed offering airline travel advice. Dogbert recommends smuggling a weapon aboard and refusing to put the seat upright, framing it as defending one's rights. Dilbert points out that every tip would land him in jail.
punchline: Dogbert's deliberately terrible, illegal advice is dismissed with a mock-childish accusation that Dilbert is simply being too negative.
summary: A pooch gives his packing owner a string of ridiculous flying tips, all of which would end in a prison cell, and then blames him for griping.

punchline: Wally treats a petty, potentially lethal scheme against his boss as a wholesome hobby, enjoying it the way people enjoy knitting or stamp collecting.
summary: A deadpan coworker reveals he is quietly trying to asphyxiate the boss and describes the plot as a satisfying new pastime.

title: Disruptive Innovation Means Selling Things

punchline: Consultant jargon like 'disruptive innovation' is just a fancy rewording of common sense, and the consultant's real value is in the fancy wording that justifies his fee.
summary: A consultant dresses up the obvious advice to make things customers want in buzzwords, and a manager realizes the only real difference is the sales pitch.

summary: A dim manager treats a coworker's sarcastic coin joke as real wisdom and plans to impress the board with it, to her secret delight.

setting: Office cubicles and a hallway outside the new hire's cubicle
situation: A bored bald coworker with glasses decides to stalk the new hire as a way to pass the time. He walks over and finds a line of men already waiting, one clutching a bouquet, with a forty-five minute wait. He then reflects that when romance is involved, it helps to have a backup plan.
punchline: The new hire is so attractive that a long line of suitors already waits to woo her, so the stalker needs a plan B, such as a different approach or a different target.
summary: A restless office worker plans to pursue the newcomer, only to discover that a whole queue of admirers got there first.

file: 2004/2004-10-15_new voice presdient_right and wrong_customers project_hate the most_charge for time.gif
title: Ethics VP Advises Billing Hated Customers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new vice president of ethics will help you decide what's right and wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When we talk to him, what customer's project should we charge for our time?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whichever one we hate the most.

situation: The Boss announces to the team that a new vice president of ethics will help them decide right from wrong. Dilbert asks which customer's project they should bill their time to, and the Boss answers that it should be whichever customer they hate the most.
punchline: The supposed ethics guidance is really about deciding which customer to overbill, and the Boss's criterion of simply hating the customer shows how little ethics has to do with it.
summary: A manager's promise of ethical guidance turns into advice to pad the bill of the least-liked client.

file: 2004/2004-07-30_car_late_cold_car wouldn't start_warm out_wind chill factor_no actual car_lied. boss_excuse.gif
title: Wally's Wind-Chill Excuse Exposed

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm late because my car wouldn't start in the cold.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's warm outside.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There's a little thing called the wind-chill factor. Hello-o-o-o!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That was wrong on so many levels.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Someday I gotta get me a car.

setting: Boss's office and a hallway in the office
situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells the boss he was late because his car wouldn't start in the cold. When the boss points out that it's warm outside, Wally condescendingly cites the wind-chill factor. Afterward Dilbert remarks that the excuse was wrong on many levels, and Wally admits he doesn't own a car.
punchline: Wally's excuse fails twice over: the weather is warm, wind chill doesn't affect cars, and he doesn't even own a car to blame.
summary: A lazy employee invents a car-trouble alibi for lateness that collapses once it's revealed he has no car at all.

file: 2004/2004-04-06_no frills airline_$23 run to destinations_crazy stuff_saliva.gif
title: Dogbert's Extreme No-Frills Airline

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I plan to start my own no-frills airline.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For only $23, I'll let people hold out their arms and run to their destinations.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And they won't be allowed to eat or swallow their own saliva.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert, sitting on the couch next to a robed Dilbert who sips from a mug, describes his plan for a no-frills airline. He explains that for $23 customers can hold out their arms and run to their destinations. He then adds that passengers will not even be allowed to swallow their own saliva. Dilbert stays silent throughout.
punchline: Dogbert takes airline cost-cutting to absurd extremes by offering no plane at all and charging customers for the privilege of running with their arms out, then stripping away even basic bodily functions as a further austerity measure.
summary: Dogbert pitches a budget airline so stripped down that customers simply flap their arms and sprint, with even swallowing banned.

title: Wally's Plausible Password Excuse

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, do you have the approved vendor list?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's on the net. The password is "Wally."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hmm...you always say information is on the net when I know it's not. Yet, by mentioning a password, it sounds plausible.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So...first I'll find out that the password has changed. Then I'll find out that the list is out of date. What am I forgetting?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: User name.

situation: Alice asks Wally for the approved vendor list and he claims it is online behind a password. Alice recognizes his habit of falsely saying information is on the net and predicts the excuses he will use next. Wally smugly sips his coffee and supplies the one she missed: the user name.
punchline: Alice lays out Wally's entire chain of stalling excuses, and Wally cheerfully adds one more, proving he is unashamedly working the system to avoid doing any work.
summary: A coworker anticipates every dodge a lazy colleague might use to avoid producing a document, and he happily hands her another one.

title: Blinded by the Boss's Obviousness

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: It's temporary blindness caused by your boss's flashes of the obvious.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Let Dogbert guide you for a few days. And here's a prescription to make you dopey.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Whatever.

setting: A doctor's examination room, then a city sidewalk
situation: A doctor shines a penlight in Dilbert's eyes and diagnoses temporary blindness caused by his boss's flashes of the obvious. He suggests Dogbert guide Dilbert for a few days and prescribes medication to make him dopey. Outside, a blinded Dilbert gropes into the air and asks Dogbert if it is time to start, and Dogbert indifferently answers.
punchline: The boss's stating of the obvious is so dazzling it literally blinds Dilbert, and the prescribed remedy of being made dopey, guided by an apathetic Dogbert, is no better than the condition.
summary: A physician blames an employee's sudden blindness on his manager's dazzling statements of the self-evident and sends him off drugged and led by his dog.

title: Misleading Or Incomprehensible Explanation Choice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell me again what the issue is.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you want the simple but misleading explanation or the one you won't understand?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Either one is good; I wasn't planning on listening.

setting: The Boss's office, across a desk
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to explain a technical problem again. Dilbert offers him a choice between a simple but misleading explanation and an accurate one the Boss won't understand. The Boss says either is fine because he had no intention of listening.
punchline: The Boss admits he asked for an explanation he never intended to listen to, making the whole exchange pointless.
summary: Offered a choice of two useless explanations, a manager cheerfully confesses he was never going to pay attention anyway.

title: Dogbert's Manipulation Advice Backfires Healthily

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can manipulate people by lying about what other people said.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If your victim goes to the source and discovers your treachery, say, "Of course he tells YOU that."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your advice doesn't sound healthy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's not what the Mayo Clinic said.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert sits on the couch beside Dilbert and coaches him on manipulating people by lying about what others said, including a ready-made excuse if the victim checks with the source. Dilbert, holding a drink, objects that the advice sounds unhealthy. Dogbert answers by falsely claiming the Mayo Clinic said otherwise.
punchline: Dogbert immediately applies his own manipulation technique to Dilbert, lying about what a respected authority said to defend his unethical advice.
summary: A scheming dog tutors his owner in deceit and then uses that very trick to brush off the owner's doubts.

file: 2004/2004-12-24_marketing needs volunteers_ads stimulate_people brains_cat scan_see coming.gif
title: Volunteering for a Cat Scan

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Marketing needs volunteers for a study about how our ads stimulate people's brains.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who among us would like to get a cat scan?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Okay, seriously, who didn't see this coming?

situation: The Boss announces that Marketing needs volunteers for a study on how ads stimulate people's brains, then reveals the study involves a cat scan. Carol asks who didn't see this coming, while Catbert, the evil cat, sits quietly at the table.
punchline: The Boss's pun on 'cat scan' makes the volunteer request sound like a trap involving the cat at the table, and Carol sarcastically notes that everyone could have predicted the joke.
summary: A manager recruits meeting attendees for a brain study that turns out to be a cat scan, to the exasperation of his staff.

title: Blind Optimism Meets Prostate Growth

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Blah, blah, blah, blah, blah.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (thought)
transcript.text: I wasn't listening. I'll try some optimism. That works in every situation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope we'll see record growth!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: In my prostate?

situation: A coworker drones on in a meeting while Dilbert, who has stopped listening, privately decides to fake engagement with generic optimism. He cheerfully says he hopes for record growth, but the coworker had actually been discussing his own prostate problem.
punchline: Dilbert's habit of responding with canned positivity without listening backfires when 'record growth' turns out to refer to the coworker's enlarged prostate.
summary: Tuning out a colleague's talk, Dilbert fires off a stock cheerful remark that turns out to be wildly inappropriate for the topic at hand.

title: Four-Hour Meeting, Zero Notes Taken

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This was a productive four-hour leadership meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like one of you to type up your notes and send an e-mail to the entire company.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Musical notes float above the silent attendees.)

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one took notes?

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: I didn't have a pen.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, no problem. Does anyone remember what we decided?

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: We agreed to increase... something.

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: No, decrease something.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Never mind. Let's try it again on Thursday at 8 a.m.

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: When is the next leadership meeting?

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: I should have written that down.

setting: Conference room where a leadership meeting is held, ending in a manager's office
situation: After a four-hour leadership meeting, the Boss calls it productive and asks someone to write up the notes for the whole company. Nobody took notes, and nobody can recall what was decided, so the Boss schedules the same meeting again for Thursday at 8 a.m. One attendee then asks when the next meeting is and admits she should have written it down.
punchline: Four hours of meeting produced no decisions and no records, so the only remedy management can think of is to repeat the meeting, which is probably just as pointless.
summary: A marathon management meeting leaves everyone unable to recall its outcome, so the boss simply orders a repeat session.

title: Dilbert Grows Beard Waiting on Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I decided to shave off the beard I grew when I was waiting for my boss to get off the phone.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Beard? I hadn't noticed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This will take awhile, so I'll wait until time slows to a crawl and do it then.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did I ever tell you about my first job as an envelope licker?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click

setting: Dilbert's home, then a conference room meeting
situation: Dilbert, sporting a huge white beard grown during a long wait for his boss to finish a phone call, tells Dogbert he plans to shave it off. He says he'll do it when time slows to a crawl, which in the final panel happens as the boss begins a dull anecdote in a meeting. Dilbert sits there with the beard, shaver in hand, ready to start.
punchline: Dilbert knows that the boss's boring stories make time drag, so a meeting is the perfect moment to schedule a lengthy chore like shaving off a giant beard.
summary: A man with an enormous beard saves his shaving for the one place where time reliably crawls: listening to his boss ramble.

title: Dogbert Hires Unethical Scientists for Infomercial

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My wealth-building system has been verified by actual scientists.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Where can I find an unethical scientist?

transcript.speaker: Mad Scientist
transcript.text: And if I'm too busy, my human clone can do your infomercial.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Good prices.

setting: Dilbert's living room and a table where Dogbert meets two scientists
situation: Dogbert is writing the sales pitch for his get-rich-quick scheme and realizes that it needs scientific backing. He asks where to find an unethical scientist, then meets with one who offers to have his human clone appear in the infomercial. Dogbert approves of the low prices.
punchline: Dogbert doesn't want real science, only a scientist willing to lie for cash, and he is delighted that the bargain-priced one even includes a human clone as a bonus.
summary: Needing a scientist to endorse his dubious money-making system, Dogbert shops around for one with flexible morals and finds a bargain.

title: Dilbert Wonders If He's Oblivious

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've noticed that all of my problems are caused by other people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yet it seems so unlikely that other people would cause me so much discomfort while I never bother anyone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it possible that I'm oblivious to my effect on others?

situation: Dilbert stands next to the couch and muses aloud about his problems while Dogbert sits on the couch. Over three panels he reasons that other people cause all his trouble, then questions that logic and wonders whether he himself is the problem. Dogbert ignores him and is asleep by the last panel.
punchline: Dilbert only pauses to wonder whether he is the problem after rambling on, and Dogbert has fallen asleep, which suggests he is indeed an unintentionally tiresome presence.
summary: A man talks himself into suspecting he may be the difficult one, while his dog dozes off in the middle of his monologue.

file: 2004/2004-07-04_created work_email him_end the madness_meeting with boss_pulling plugs_request.gif
title: Carol Bans the Boss's Meetings

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Carol, I need ten minutes on the Pointy-Haired Boss' schedule.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I don't let him have meetings anymore.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Every time he had a meeting it just created more work for me.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: It was always "Carol, get me a file," and "Carol, schedule another meeting."

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Obviously I had to put an end to the madness.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess I could e-mail him.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You could try.

setting: Office cubicles and the Boss's office
situation: Dilbert asks Carol, the Boss's assistant, to book ten minutes on the Boss's calendar. Carol explains that she no longer lets the Boss have meetings because each one generated extra work for her. In the last panel the Boss is shown at his desk with his computer and phone cables yanked out, so Dilbert's plan to email him is doomed.
punchline: Carol has solved her workload problem by unplugging the Boss's computer and phone, so he is effectively unreachable.
summary: A frustrated assistant has quietly cut off her manager's communications so he can no longer generate tasks for her.

title: Hiding Disguised as Philosophy

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I'm cruising into my fifth month with no written objectives.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Some philosophers would say that having no objectives means I'm free to help any team that asks.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: My personal philosophy is more along the lines of hiding.

situation: At a meeting table, Phil brags that he has gone five months without any written objectives. He first offers a flattering philosophical spin, saying having no objectives frees him to help any team, then admits that what he is really doing is hiding. Dilbert and another man sit beside him listening.
punchline: Phil dresses up avoiding accountability as a lofty philosophy, then candidly admits his real strategy is simply to hide from work and evaluation.
summary: A coworker who has dodged assigned goals for months first spins his situation as noble flexibility, then cheerfully confesses he is just keeping out of sight.

title: Wally Claims Emptiness, Gets Hungry

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, did you complain to Human Resources about my off-color e-mail joke?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes. I was psychologically damaged by your mirth. Now I'm an empty shell of a man.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You've ALWAYS been an empty shell of a man!!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This is making me hungry.

situation: Alice confronts Wally, asking whether he reported her off-color e-mail joke to Human Resources. Wally calmly admits it and claims her humor left him psychologically damaged and an empty shell of a man. Alice angrily retorts that he has always been one, and Wally merely remarks that this is making him hungry.
punchline: Wally treats being called an empty shell as a hollow-food remark, and his deadpan hunger shows he is unbothered by both his supposed trauma and Alice's insult, which exposes the complaint as insincere.
summary: After reporting a coworker's crude email to HR, a lazy employee shrugs off her furious insult by musing about being hungry.

file: 2004/2004-10-31_senior vice president_impress_chummy with intern_slacking slacker_good motivation.gif
title: Boss Berates Intern for Senior VP

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The new senior vice president will be at my meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope to impress him with my leadership skills.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh-oh. Underling alert.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't be seen getting chummy with an intern.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Please don't try to make conversation. Don't, don't, don't, don't, don't.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Did you do anything fun this weekend?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here he comes!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Get back to work, you slacking slacker!!!

transcript.speaker: Senior Vice President
transcript.text: Good motivating! If he blows his nose with his necktie, you're my new vice president.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Waaa!!!

situation: The Boss waits for the new senior vice president to arrive at his meeting and nervously tries to look like a strong leader. He silently begs the intern not to chat with him, but the intern innocently asks about his weekend. The Boss panics and yells at the intern for slacking in front of the senior executive.
punchline: The senior vice president is impressed by the Boss's cruel treatment of an innocent intern and rewards him, implying that bullying subordinates is what passes for good leadership.
summary: A manager desperate to look tough in front of a visiting executive screams at a friendly intern and is applauded for his supposed motivational skills.

title: Dogbert's Horrifying Extreme Makeover Business

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going into the extreme make-over business.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm planning to take it to the next level.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You'd look good with antlers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And the nose has to go.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Go?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your tiny ears are out of proportion.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: These are ears.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll also rearrange your fat so you can't see it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll toss in a few extras after you're unconscious.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No charge.

transcript.speaker: Monstrous Client
transcript.text: Guess how old I am!

setting: Dilbert's living room, then Dogbert's makeover office and a restaurant
situation: Dogbert announces to Dilbert that he is entering the extreme makeover business. He then lectures a client on what he will change, including antlers, the nose and the ears, and promises unrequested extras while the client is unconscious. In the final panel the client has been turned into a grotesque monkey-like creature with antlers, drinking wine on a date.
punchline: Dogbert's makeovers are wildly invasive and unauthorized, leaving the client a bizarre antlered monster who still behaves as if he had received an ordinary cosmetic upgrade.
summary: A scheming dog reshapes a customer into an antlered freak and the creature cheerfully goes on a date.

title: Dilbert Negotiates a Lopsided Contract

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Negotiations

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So far we've agreed that my company will take all the expenses and legal liabilities.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your company will take all of the revenue, patents and public credit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But where it says I'll dig you a swimming pool with my bare hands, I will not do that.

transcript.speaker: Negotiator
transcript.text: You win! You can use a spoon.

setting: A negotiating table in a meeting room
situation: Dilbert reads aloud from a contract during negotiations with a man in a suit, listing terms that saddle his company with all expenses and liabilities while the other party takes all revenue, patents and credit. He accepts all of that but draws the line at digging a swimming pool by hand. The other negotiator gleefully 'concedes' by letting him use a spoon.
punchline: Dilbert pushes back on one absurd clause after meekly accepting hugely unfair terms, and the counterparty's 'generous' concession is still ridiculous, showing how badly he is being fleeced.
summary: After agreeing to shoulder every cost and risk of a one-sided deal, a man finally objects to one silly clause and wins only a tiny, pointless concession.

title: Sued Former Employer Over Poor Judgment

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why did you leave your last job?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: They told me that I have incredibly poor judgment.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: So I sued them.

situation: The Boss interviews a job candidate across a desk and asks why he left his previous job. The candidate says his former employer told him he has incredibly poor judgment, then reveals that he sued them in response.
punchline: Suing his old employer over a comment about his poor judgment is itself an example of poor judgment, so he unwittingly proves them right.
summary: An interviewee explains that he quit after being accused of bad judgment, then unwittingly confirms the charge by describing his lawsuit.

title: Faxing Alice's Voice Line

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hello? This is Alice.

transcript.speaker: Fax Tone
transcript.text: Beeeep beeeep

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You are faxing to my voice line again, you #!!%*

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How often do you fax to her voice line?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It depends if she's been bad.

setting: Office cubicle and a nearby fax machine area
situation: Alice answers her phone and hears only fax tones, then angrily accuses the caller of faxing her voice line again. Dilbert asks a coworker standing at the fax machine how often he does this, and the coworker reveals he does it deliberately.
punchline: The coworker's repeated mistake is actually deliberate harassment, used as punishment whenever Alice has annoyed him.
summary: A man with a fax machine turns out to be torturing a colleague with screeching fax noises on purpose, using it as a petty form of retribution.

title: Dogbert Demands Conflicts of Interest

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll recommend your stock to the public, but first I need some conflicts of interest to make it worthwhile.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For example, I'll need to get your investment banking business.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And you need to merge with my other client that makes poison waffles.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a stock analyst, tells the Boss he will recommend the company's stock to the public only if he gets conflicts of interest in return. He asks for the company's investment banking business and then for a merger with another client that makes poison waffles. The Boss agrees to everything without objection.
punchline: The corrupt stock analyst piles on absurd demands, including merging with a poison waffle maker, and the clueless Boss agrees each time, mocking how conflicts of interest corrupted Wall Street analyst recommendations.
summary: A scheming stock analyst extracts ever more outrageous concessions from a compliant executive in exchange for publicly promoting his company's shares.

file: 2004/2004-07-28_founder of compnay_tug up_copper wire_replaced tombstone_huge magnet_business practivces_spin in grave_generate electricity.gif
title: Founder Spinning in Grave Power Plant

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We dug up the founder of our company and wrapped him in copper wire.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then we replaced his tombstone with a huge magnet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: With any luck, our business practices will make him spin in his grave and generate electricity.

setting: Conference room, with presentation slides shown in the first two panels
situation: Dilbert gives a presentation to The Boss and another executive about an energy project. He explains that the company's founder was dug up, wrapped in copper wire, and his tombstone replaced with a giant magnet. He hopes the company's business practices will make the founder spin in his grave and generate power.
punchline: The company's business practices are so bad that Dilbert expects them to make the dead founder spin in his grave, and he plans to harness that motion as a power source.
summary: Dilbert proposes turning the company founder's corpse into a generator, powered by his horror at how the business is now run.

file: 2004/2004-12-14_stock guy_conflicts of interest_knocked out_fist down throat_violence_crime.gif
title: Murdered Analyst Was Our Only Buy

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I didn't like the way he was looking at me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This isn't good.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He was the only stock analyst who had a "buy" recommendation on our company.

transcript.speaker: Carol

transcript.text: Where will we find another one with so much conflict of interest??!

The Boss is initially worried, then explains that the analyst was the only one giving the company a "buy" rating. His real concern is finding another analyst with such a conflict of interest.
punchline: The Boss is less bothered by the apparent violence than by losing the one analyst whose favorable rating was bought through a conflict of interest.
summary: After a woman does away with a stock analyst, her boss mourns not the man but the loss of his biased, company-friendly rating.

title: Becoming Indispensable Through Annoying Habits

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've decided to become indispensable to the company.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Indispensable employees can get away with outrageously annoying behavior.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're already pretty annoying.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've been reading up on crushed ice chomping.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells Dilbert he plans to become indispensable to the company, explaining that indispensable employees can get away with outrageously annoying behavior. Dilbert points out that Wally is already pretty annoying. Wally replies that he has been researching crushed ice chomping as a way to get even more annoying.
punchline: Wally's goal of becoming indispensable is just an excuse to be more annoying, and he is already so irritating that he is studying new ways to escalate it.
summary: A lazy coworker plans to earn job security so he can unleash even worse irritating habits, and is already studying how to chew ice noisily.

title: Records Retention Policy Knocks Boss Out

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: To defend against lawsuits, our records retention policy has been updated to include this...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: BAM!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What was I talking about?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The records retention policy.

situation: The Boss announces that the records retention policy has been updated to defend against lawsuits, then slams his head onto the conference table. When he sits up dazed, he has forgotten what he was talking about, and a bald coworker in glasses reminds him it was the records retention policy.
punchline: The updated records retention policy apparently involves literally knocking employees unconscious so they can't remember anything, which is a way to avoid having incriminating memories in a lawsuit.
summary: To protect the company in court, the meeting leader bashes his own head on the table and promptly forgets everything he was saying.

file: 2004/2004-11-09_warning lables_on donuts_high calorie donuts_will kill you_tastes great_choked to death.gif
title: Deadly Doughnut Warning Label Suggestion

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The government says we have to put warning labels on our forty-thousand calorie, shard-filled doughnuts product.

transcript.text: How about: "Warning! This product will kill you but that's okay because it tastes great!"
