transcript.text: It looks like he choked on some sort of warning label.

setting: Conference room, then the scene of a death
situation: The Boss tells Dogbert, acting as a consultant, that the government requires warning labels on the company's extremely fatty, shard-filled doughnuts. Dogbert suggests a blunt label admitting the product will kill you but tastes great. In the last panel, police stand over the Boss's body, sprawled beside a giant spiky doughnut with a label stuck in his throat.
punchline: The Boss, who ignores the real danger of his own deadly product, ends up dead himself, apparently from choking on the warning label, a darkly ironic outcome that blames the label instead of the doughnuts.
summary: A manager asks for help with a mandatory safety notice on his lethal pastries and soon turns up dead, with the police blaming the notice itself.

title: Merging With Worst Division

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have a plan to avoid paying division performance bonuses.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll merge our group with the worst division so our average performance is lower. Hee-hee!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It should be easy because every division manager is already begging to merge with me.

setting: Lunch table in an office or break room
situation: The Boss eats a sandwich across a table from Catbert, the evil HR director, while explaining his scheme to dodge division performance bonuses. He plans to merge his group with the worst-performing division to drag down the average. He cheerfully notes that every other division manager already wants to merge with him.
punchline: The Boss thinks his bonus-avoidance scheme is clever, but the fact that all the other managers are begging to merge with him suggests they all have the same plan, and his group is probably the high performer being exploited.
summary: A manager gleefully plots to dilute his division's results by absorbing a failing unit, without grasping why everyone else wants to join him.

file: 2004/2004-11-20_biggest deficit_inability handle criticism_stupid misperceptions_argue with smarter people.gif
title: Boss Criticizes Alice's Criticism Handling

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your biggest defect continues to be your inability to handle criticism.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can't argue with his stupid misperception without proving it true.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you argue with people who are much smarter than yourself.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

setting: The Boss's office during a performance review
situation: The Boss gives Alice a performance review, telling her that her biggest flaw is that she can't take criticism. Alice silently fumes, realizing that any rebuttal would confirm his claim. The Boss then adds that she argues with people much smarter than herself, and Alice screams in frustration.
punchline: The Boss's review is a catch-22 that makes Alice's anger look like proof of his criticism, while he smugly claims to be smarter than her, which is the opposite of the truth.
summary: A manager's smug appraisal leaves his furious employee trapped, since objecting would only demonstrate the flaw he accuses her of having.

title: Optometrist Preys on Optimistic Customers

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've decided to become an optometrist for near-sighted visionaries.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They're ideal customers because they never expect the worst.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Which price am I most likely to charge you?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: The low one!

setting: Dilbert's bedroom, then an optometrist's exam room
situation: Dogbert, sitting on Dilbert's bed, announces his plan to become an optometrist who serves near-sighted visionaries. He explains that optimistic people make ideal customers. In the exam room, Dogbert asks a customer which price he will charge, and the customer cheerfully guesses the low one.
punchline: Dogbert plans to overcharge naive optimists, and the customer's confident guess of the low price proves he never expects the worst.
summary: Dogbert sets up an eye-care business aimed at gullible, hopeful clients who will happily walk into being overcharged.

file: 2004/2004-04-19_real estate_sell house_agent_doesn't know maybe_moving fast_control process_escrow closes.gif

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll be the real estate agent.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I said maybe.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A good real estate agent doesn't know the meaning of that word.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Things are moving too fast! I've lost control of the process!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Pack your stuff, waffler. Escrow closes in ten days.

situation: Dilbert casually muses over coffee that he might sell his house and buy a newer one. Dogbert immediately volunteers to be his real estate agent and ignores Dilbert's hedging. Within moments Dilbert panics that the sale is moving too fast, and Dogbert tells him escrow closes in ten days.
punchline: Dogbert, as an aggressive real estate agent, treats Dilbert's tentative 'maybe' as a firm commitment and railroads him into a rapid sale, mocking his indecision.
summary: A tentative musing about moving gets steamrolled into a done deal by a pushy pet agent who refuses to acknowledge hesitation.

title: Stock Analyst Meets Angry Tina

situation: During a meeting, Tina grows hostile toward a stranger who keeps asking her questions and threatens him with violence while the Boss watches calmly. She then attacks the man, and the Boss casually remarks that she has met the company's stock analyst.
punchline: The Boss is completely unbothered that an employee is assaulting a visitor, noting only that the victim is the stock analyst, implying the company expects hostility toward analysts.
summary: A prickly employee threatens and then pummels an unfamiliar questioner, who turns out to be the firm's stock analyst, to the Boss's mild amusement.

title: Boss Bribes Employees to Lie

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our bonuses will depend on the results of the employee attitude survey.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If we boost our morale rank, we'll get bigger bonuses.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Get it? All you have to do is say you're happy and you get money.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wink wink wink

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You want us to lie?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No-o-o-o! Heaven forbid. Absolutely no lying.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But if you did lie, imagine the things you could buy with that money.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll hand out the surveys and you can let your conscience guide you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is "paradise" too over the top?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm going to lie me up a new couch!

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss tells his team that their bonuses depend on the employee attitude survey results, and winks while hinting that they should simply say they're happy. When Dilbert asks if they're being told to lie, the Boss denies it while dangling the money, then hands out the surveys. The employees start planning exaggerated answers and what to buy with the bonus.
punchline: The Boss officially forbids lying while openly encouraging it with a financial incentive, so the survey results become meaningless and the employees happily game them.
summary: A manager winks his way through a thinly veiled order to fake glowing survey answers in exchange for bigger paychecks, and his staff eagerly takes the hint.

title: Underpaid Assistant Plots Boss's Demise

transcript.speaker: Boss's Secretary
transcript.text: You're still alive?? How can this be??

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Boss's Secretary
transcript.text: Nothing! Never mind! I don't know anything about a deadly plot!

transcript.speaker: Boss's Secretary
transcript.text: It's his own fault for not paying me enough to afford entertainment.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Good one.

situation: The Boss's secretary is shocked to see him alive and accidentally blurts out that she expected him to be dead. When he asks what she said, she panics and denies knowing anything about a deadly plot. Afterwards she complains to a coworker that his low pay left her with nothing to do but plot against him, and the coworker approves.
punchline: The secretary treats plotting her boss's murder as a cheap hobby, blaming his stingy pay for leaving her unable to afford any other entertainment.
summary: A badly paid assistant accidentally gives away her scheme to kill her boss, then shrugs it off as a pastime he drove her to.

title: Stock Rises When Boss Sits Still

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your stock just plunged on the news that you're going to acquire another company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Have you noticed that your stock goes down whenever you do anything?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll buy a few shares if you'll agree to sit motionlessly in your cubicle.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert, sitting on an end table beside a lamp, tells a silent Dilbert that his company's stock fell after news of an acquisition. He points out that the stock drops whenever Dilbert does anything, then offers to buy shares if Dilbert promises to sit motionless in his cubicle.
punchline: Dogbert implies that Dilbert's actions are so harmful to the company that the stock is only worth buying if he does nothing at all.
summary: Dogbert notes that any activity by Dilbert sinks the share price, so he proposes investing only if Dilbert stays perfectly still at work.

title: Dogbert Teaches Recognizing Boredom

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's School for the Socially Oblivious

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Today I'll teach you to recognize when you're boring.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is called a yawn. When you see one, stop talking about yourself.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Breakout session

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: And then I chipped it right onto the green!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Look, look!

setting: Dogbert's classroom, with a breakout session area
situation: Dogbert runs a school for the socially oblivious and teaches students to spot signs of boredom, using a yawn as the example. In the breakout session, a man keeps happily recounting a golf shot while the woman he is talking to yawns openly. Dogbert points out the yawn to the man.
punchline: The man gets a perfect, obvious yawn from his listener yet keeps talking about his golf game, showing he's hopelessly oblivious despite the lesson.
summary: A lesson on noticing yawns is immediately put to the test as a golf-obsessed bore drones on while his partner yawns in his face.

file: 2004/2004-12-20_online ereume_older chubby men_key words_married men_job offers_cousin_advice_one line job hunting.gif
title: Resume Keywords Attract Unusual Admirers

setting: Outdoors on a sidewalk beside a hedge
situation: Dilbert walks outside with a young woman with a bob haircut, who explains her job-hunting breakthrough. She added key words to her online resume saying she is attracted to older, chubby, married men with coffee-stained teeth. Dilbert objects, and she retorts that she has received six thousand job offers.
punchline: Her ethically dubious keyword stuffing worked spectacularly, so the flood of job offers (presumably from the kind of men she described) undercuts Dilbert's moral objection.
summary: A job seeker boasts that a bizarre line added to her online resume produced a deluge of employment offers, silencing a disapproving friend.

transcript.speaker: Feral Employee
transcript.text: French fry.

punchline: His dumpster dive produced nothing useful: the only thing he found was a french fry, which he presents as if it answers the question about the product specs.
summary: A scavenging coworker raids the Marketing department's trash for missing documentation and comes back with fast food leftovers instead.

punchline: Wally implies he has actually been watching online adult videos, which is why the 'actors' looked so happy, rather than an actual training course.
summary: A slacker employee's boast about finishing mandatory compliance training unravels when his boss reveals the course doesn't exist, hinting at what he was really viewing.

punchline: The Boss's ordinary phone call drags on so long that Dilbert, left in anxious suspense, thinks time has stopped, and the caption jokes that frozen people look just like the Boss on the phone.
summary: A dreaded summons turns into an agonizing wait when the boss takes a phone call, leaving the employee convinced that time has frozen.

situation: A coworker invites Dilbert to lunch, and Dilbert says he would rather go alone. The coworker laughs it off and insists Dilbert would miss a great opportunity. punchline: The friendly lunch invitation was a cover for a pushy pyramid-style sales pitch, so Dilbert's wish to eat alone was justified and he would rather die than sit through it.
summary: A cheerful coworker lures Dilbert into a meal only to hawk a dubious marketing scheme tied to a religious diet, leaving Dilbert begging for an end.

punchline: The self-proclaimed genius who expects to revolutionize invention can't be bothered to press the power button, dismissing it as 'hardware.'

transcript.text: Look through this solid block of wood.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is this better or worse?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Better.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I foresee forty quarters of growth.

transcript.speaker: Meeting attendee
transcript.text: Hey, new glasses?

setting: Dogbert's optometrist office, then a conference room meeting
situation: Dogbert, working as an optometrist for visionary executives, has the Boss look through a solid block of wood and asks whether it is better or worse. The Boss says it is better. In the next scene the Boss sits at a conference table wearing the wooden block over his eyes and confidently predicts forty quarters of growth while a coworker asks if he has new glasses.
punchline: Executives who claim to have vision are literally blinded, yet their forecasts sound confident and nobody questions them or the absurd wooden block on their face.
summary: A dog-run eye clinic fits an executive with a wooden block that he swears sharpens his foresight, and his colleagues barely notice.

title: Tech Support Blames Someone Else

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is Dogbert's Tech Support. Your problem is caused by another company's product or services.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Shouldn't I tell you my problem before you determine the cause?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay, let's pretend that will change my answer.

situation: Dogbert, working as a tech support agent with a headset, answers a call by immediately announcing that the caller's problem is caused by another company's product or services. The customer, holding a phone, points out that he hasn't even described his problem yet. Dogbert sarcastically agrees to humor him by pretending the details might matter.
punchline: Dogbert's tech support always blames a third party regardless of the problem, and he only pretends to entertain the idea that the customer's actual issue could change his verdict.
summary: A support agent pronounces a verdict on a caller's unknown problem before hearing it, then reluctantly feigns openness when challenged.

title: Boss Lures Dilbert Into Trap

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How could you tell a vendor about our reorganization before you tell your own staff?!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: (thought) Scoot.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Come into my office and we can discuss it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaaa!!! It's a trick!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: (thought) C'mon phone, ring!!!

setting: Office hallway and the Boss's office
situation: Dilbert angrily confronts the Boss for telling a vendor about a reorganization before informing his own staff. The Boss, secretly wanting to escape, invites Dilbert into his office to discuss it. Dilbert realizes it is a trick, and the Boss sits at his desk hoping the phone will ring to rescue him.
punchline: The Boss avoids accountability by luring Dilbert into a pointless 'discussion' while desperately hoping a phone call will let him dodge the conversation entirely.
summary: A manager dodges an employee's complaint about being left out of the loop by stalling and wishing for an interruption.

title: The Boss's Terrible Password Attempts

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now what?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Create a password that's at least six characters long with a mix of letters and numbers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How about 123?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh, no.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It has to include letters and be at least six characters long.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How about ABC?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Letters and numbers and at least six characters long!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Foursome?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

setting: The Boss's office, at his computer
situation: Dilbert stands over the Boss's shoulder while he tries to set up a new password. The Boss repeatedly proposes passwords that fail the stated rules, such as 123 and ABC, even as Dilbert patiently restates the requirements. Finally the Boss offers a suggestive word, and Dilbert cries out in frustration.
punchline: After failing to grasp the simple password rules, the Boss proposes 'Foursome?' as a password, which still fails the requirements and also shows his crude, clueless mindset, driving Dilbert to despair.
summary: A clueless manager keeps suggesting laughably weak passwords while an increasingly frazzled employee tries to guide him through the basic rules.

title: Retyping the Boss's Prescription Directions

transcript.speaker: The Boss's assistant
transcript.text: I have a question for the ethics hotline.

transcript.speaker: The Boss's assistant
transcript.text: Is it okay to retype the directions on my boss's prescription medication?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I know I can't do this next thing because I've tried.

setting: Office desk and the Boss's home chair
situation: The Boss's assistant holds a pill bottle and phones the company ethics hotline to ask whether she may retype the directions on her boss's prescription medication. In the last panel the Boss, shirtless on a chair and holding his pill bottle, says he cannot do some next thing because he has already tried.
punchline: The Boss's medication directions apparently include a warning about something he can't do, and the assistant wants to retype them because he is so clueless that he has tried to do the forbidden thing anyway, implying the assistant is making the warning impossible to miss or misread.
summary: An assistant seeks ethical clearance to rewrite her boss's pill-bottle instructions while the half-dressed boss admits he has already tested the limits of the warnings.

title: Blinded by the Obvious

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your blinding flashes of the obvious made me sightless for three days.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope you didn't drive your car. You're not supposed to do that when you're blind.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm upsetting you.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that his blinding flashes of the obvious literally blinded him for three days. The Boss responds by solemnly hoping Dilbert didn't drive while blind, stating a patently obvious piece of advice. Dilbert clutches his head and screams, and the Boss calmly notes that he is upsetting him.
punchline: The Boss answers a complaint about his obvious statements with yet another obvious statement, and then even states the obvious fact that he is upsetting Dilbert, proving Dilbert's point.
summary: A man accuses his manager of stating the obvious so much it blinded him, and the manager promptly responds with more obvious remarks, driving him to a scream.

title: Boss Summons Demon to Avoid Decision

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh-oh, someone wants me to make a decision.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I summon the dark demon of ineffective management to smite the person who wants this decision!!!

transcript.speaker: Demon
transcript.text: Maybe I could help you make the decision.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I requested smiting.

situation: The Boss reads a note and realizes someone wants him to make a decision. Instead of deciding, he summons the dark demon of ineffective management to smite the person asking. The green demon appears and offers to help him decide, but the Boss insists he only wanted smiting.
punchline: Even a demon of ineffective management is too constructive for the Boss, who would rather have the person asking for a decision destroyed than make the decision himself.
summary: A manager conjures a fiendish creature to eliminate whoever wants a choice from him, then rejects its offer of actual assistance.

title: Cheapest Binders Are Deadly Binders

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I want you to update the safety manual and distribute it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't have much of a budget for binders, so use the cheapest ones you can find.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hello, this is "Deadly Binders, Inc." How may I injure you?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

situation: The Boss tells Wally to update and distribute the safety manual, but says there is little budget for binders so he should buy the cheapest available. Wally then phones a vendor called Deadly Binders, Inc., and is shown bandaged and wearing an eyepatch, while a coworker nearby flails with a binder stuck to his face.
punchline: Buying the cheapest binders for a safety manual leads to a supplier whose products are literally dangerous, which ironically undermines the purpose of safety.
summary: A manager's penny-pinching order for bargain binders to hold a safety manual sends his employee to a supplier whose products maim people.

file: 2004/2004-10-25_accounting_expense figures_base ten_counting system_full range_odds and even_hp printer ink_finance troll.gif
title: Accounting Troll Tastes The Spreadsheet

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Accounting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you explain these expense figures?

transcript.speaker: Accounting Troll
transcript.text: It's a base ten counting system with a full range of odd and even digits.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This isn't helping.

transcript.speaker: Accounting Troll
transcript.text: Tastes like HP printer ink...high gloss paper, four hours old.

situation: Dilbert brings the accounting troll a printout of expense figures and asks for an explanation. The troll gives a uselessly obvious description of the number system, then eats the paper and describes its flavor like a wine critic instead of explaining the numbers.
punchline: The accounting troll gives a condescendingly obvious non-answer and then treats the financial report as food, showing that accounting provides no real insight into the numbers.
summary: A troll in accounting responds to a request for help with expense numbers by lecturing on the obvious and then nibbling the report like a gourmet.

file: 2004/2004-11-07_slaes rep_nice suit_dilbert questioned_well dressed engineer_not redibilty_reverse makeover_consultant_engineers are grungie_business.gif
title: Well-Dressed Engineer Lacks Credibility

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Go with our sales rep and answer the customer's technical questions.

transcript.speaker: Sales Rep
transcript.text: Whoa! You can't go looking like that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is a nice suit!

transcript.speaker: Sales Rep
transcript.text: Exactly.

transcript.speaker: Sales Rep
transcript.text: A well-dressed engineer has no credibility!

transcript.speaker: Sales Rep
transcript.text: I'll call my reverse makeover consultant.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I'm Bob, the straight eye for the queer-looking guy.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Let's see... I'll give you my clothes... add ear hair... eyebrow extensions.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: You seem highly credible and I don't know why.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Genius.

setting: Office cubicle, then a customer meeting room
situation: The boss tells Dilbert to accompany a sales rep to answer a customer's technical questions. The sales rep objects that Dilbert's nice suit makes him look untrustworthy, so he calls in a 'reverse makeover' consultant, Bob, who dresses Dilbert in a scruffy undershirt and adds ear hair and bushy eyebrows. At the customer meeting, the scruffy Dilbert is considered highly credible.
punchline: Customers equate sloppy, unkempt appearance with technical competence, so the makeover that makes Dilbert look worse makes him seem more credible, which baffles the customer.
summary: To impress a client, a salesman has a consultant make Dilbert look disheveled, since shabby engineers are assumed to be the smart ones.

title: Dilbert's Awkward Hallway Smile Story

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh, it's a gray area social situation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do I know this guy well enough to say hi, or do I look away?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I went with an ambiguous tight-lipped smile that could be confused with a stomach ache.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your stories suck.

setting: Office hallway, then Dilbert's home talking to Dogbert
situation: Dilbert sees a coworker approaching with a coffee mug and panics about whether he knows him well enough to say hello. He nervously decides on an ambiguous tight-lipped smile. He then recounts this to Dogbert, who bluntly tells him his stories are boring.
punchline: Dilbert tells a painfully trivial story about an awkward social moment, and Dogbert bluntly points out how dull and pointless it is.
summary: A nervous engineer agonizes over how to greet a barely-known coworker, then bores his dog with the tale.

file: 2004/2004-03-31_dr. dogbert show_plastic surgery addicts_dinosaur_shut up freak.gif
title: Dogbert Advises Dinosaur Surgery Addict

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Doctor Dogbert Show

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My next guest is addicted to plastic surgery.

transcript.speaker: Guest
transcript.text: I've always liked the whole dinosaur look, so I just went for it.

transcript.speaker: Guest
transcript.text: Do you have some plainspoken advice for me?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Shut up, you freak.

situation: Dogbert hosts a talk show and introduces a guest addicted to plastic surgery. The guest, who has had himself surgically transformed into a dinosaur, explains his choice and asks for plainspoken advice. Dogbert bluntly insults him.
punchline: Asked for plainspoken advice, Dogbert delivers the blunt truth that the guest is a freak, which is arguably the most honest counsel available.
summary: A talk show host receives a request for frank advice from a man who surgically made himself look like a dinosaur and answers with a curt insult.

title: Product That Attacks Its Customer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our target market is people who don't shop carefully.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our product is designed to attack the user and force him to reorder.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We only have one customer but we've sold 10,000 units.

setting: Marketing presentation in a conference room with a screen showing a product demo
situation: Dilbert gives a product presentation, pointing at a screen that shows a customer using the product. In the first panel the customer happily listens to music on a gadget, but in the next the device clamps onto his head and he screams. By the last panel the customer is buried under a tall stack of the identical units he has been forced to reorder.
punchline: The company counts its sales as successful even though the product is so awful it attacks its one customer, who keeps reordering, so the sales numbers are meaningless.
summary: A presenter proudly explains a gadget built to assault its owner into buying replacements, boasting about huge unit sales to a single unfortunate buyer.

file: 2004/2004-12-25_bench mark results_ten minute explination_in sales_here you go.gif
title: Useless Benchmark Data, Handed Over Anyway

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Dilbert, do you have the benchmark results?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you want the ten-minute explanation of why the data are useless, or a simple "here you go"?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm in sales.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here you go.

situation: A coworker asks Dilbert for the benchmark results. Dilbert offers a choice between a ten-minute explanation of why the data are useless or simply handing them over. The coworker says he's in sales, and Dilbert hands him the printout.
punchline: Because salespeople don't care whether data is valid, only that they can use it, Dilbert hands over the flawed benchmarks without any warning.
summary: Dilbert gives a salesman worthless test data without a word of caution once he learns what the man does for a living.

file: 2004/2004-06-14_small business_need to be paid_small man_truthful_painfully honest.gif
title: Small Business Owner Begs, Then Blunders

transcript.speaker: Small Man
transcript.text: I own a small business.

transcript.speaker: Small Man
transcript.text: It's imperative that you pay us on time or else we'll go out of business.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And then you wouldn't ever need to pay...

transcript.speaker: Small Man
transcript.text: Oh, dear Lord, what have I said?!!

situation: A tiny man sitting in a big chair tells the Boss that he owns a small business and needs to be paid on time or his company will fold. The Boss, holding a coffee mug, reasons aloud that if the business closed he would never have to pay. The small man realizes with horror that he has handed the Boss a motive to pay late.
punchline: By honestly explaining that late payment would kill his business, the small man accidentally gives the Boss a reason to stall, since the Boss would then owe nothing at all.
summary: A struggling vendor's candid plea for prompt payment backfires when his customer realizes that bankrupting him would erase the debt.

title: Choosing Between Bad Management Options

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need clarification on my assignment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I use my own judgment and be forever damned if things go badly?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or should I use your advice and invite certain calamity?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Both plans have good parts.

situation: Dilbert walks into the Boss's office, holding his tie, and asks for clarification on an assignment. He lays out two options: rely on his own judgment and take the blame if it fails, or follow the Boss's advice and bring about certain disaster. The Boss cheerfully replies that both plans have good parts.
punchline: The Boss misses the point that Dilbert is calling his advice disastrous, responding with a cheerful non-answer that offers no clarification at all.
summary: An employee seeking guidance on a task is given a vacuous reply by a boss who ignores the insult baked into the question.

title: Forgiveness Over Permission, Heart Sold Online

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! How could you do this without first checking with me??!!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: My philosophy is that it's better to seek forgiveness than to ask for permission.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did he say you could rip out his heart and sell it on the Internet?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Kinda.

situation: Alice furiously confronts a coworker for acting without consulting her first. He calmly replies that it is better to seek forgiveness than ask permission. In the hallway, Dilbert asks whether the man authorized her to rip out his heart and sell it online, and Alice admits he sort of did.
punchline: Alice took the 'better to ask forgiveness than permission' philosophy to a violent extreme, literally ripping out the coworker's heart and selling it, treating his vague statement as sufficient authorization.
summary: A coworker's casual excuse about acting first and apologizing later gets turned against him in the most gruesome way imaginable.

file: 2004/2004-04-15_mother and son_cooking_cooking show_televsion_too much salt_mad mom_complaining_mom questions.gif
title: Mother Guilt-Trips Dilbert About Career

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mother
transcript.text: Have you made your mother proud by becoming a manager?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mother
transcript.text: Have you made your son proud by hosting a cooking show on television?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You could call the show "Cooking with too much salt."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mother
transcript.text: How did you get this way?

situation: Dilbert's mother, cooking at the stove, asks whether he has made her proud by becoming a manager. After he says no, she turns the question around and asks if he has made his son proud by hosting a TV cooking show. Dilbert responds that she could call her show "Cooking with too much salt," and she asks how he got to be so sarcastic.
punchline: Dilbert's mother teases him with the same guilt-trip she gets from him, and he fires back with a jab about her over-salted cooking, proving he inherited his sarcasm from her.
summary: A mother and her grown son trade pointed barbs about career pride and her heavy-handed seasoning in the kitchen.
keywords: how did you get this way

title: Forgotten Name Standoff Ends Abruptly

transcript.text: Why it's great to be an engineer

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hi, Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi...there.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He doesn't remember my name.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Say it! Say my name!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Now he'll be forced to introduce me. Hee-hee!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Am I interrupting anything?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's awkward for you now. Ha ha! Squirm, you name forgetter.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The pressure to introduce me must be killing you. Ha ha!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Follow me.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Who was that guy?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: A coworker greets Dilbert, who responds awkwardly because he has forgotten the man's name. The coworker gleefully waits for Dilbert to squirm when a woman approaches and he'll have to introduce him. Dilbert instead asks the woman about hardware specs and walks off with her, ignoring the coworker entirely.
punchline: Dilbert sidesteps the social awkwardness by completely ignoring the coworker, so effectively that he later pretends the man never existed, leaving the coworker's scheme to humiliate him backfiring.
summary: A smug colleague plots to embarrass Dilbert over a forgotten name, but Dilbert simply walks away with a coworker and acts as though the man was never there.

file: 2004/2004-12-26_spreadsheet for accuracy_impenetrable jumble_poorly organized_cryptic labels_simple document_ratio of returns_sales taxes_roprtgresta_organizing_taxes_coulumns.gif
title: Checking a Spreadsheet Nobody Can Read

transcript.text: Can you check my spreadsheet for accuracy?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I only need you to check it for accuracy.

transcript.text: I don't think accuracy matters if no one can tell what it's for.

transcript.speaker: Coworker

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's clearly labeled "ROPRTGRESTA."

transcript.text: What about the other 80 columns?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What the #*%!?

transcript.text: And Dilbert found no inaccuracies.

setting: Office cubicles, then the Boss's office
situation: A coworker asks Dilbert to check his spreadsheet for accuracy, but Dilbert says it is an unreadable mess of cryptic labels. The coworker insists it is simple and explains one column, whose label is an unintelligible abbreviation, while Dilbert points out there are 80 more. The coworker then reports to the Boss that Dilbert found no inaccuracies, leaving the Boss baffled.
punchline: The coworker twists Dilbert's refusal to verify an incomprehensible spreadsheet into a clean bill of health, so the Boss is told the data has been checked and found accurate.
summary: A man demands a review of his baffling data sheet, then spins the reviewer's complaints into a report that no mistakes were found.

file: 2004/2004-05-01_invoices_unauthorized dedcutions_standard industry practice_dance like chickens_chicken are funny.gif
title: Dogbert Teaches Supplier Bullying Tactics

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can rob your small suppliers by making unauthorized deductions from their invoices.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When they complain, say it's a standard industry practice and threaten to take your business elsewhere!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then make them dance like chickens!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ha ha!! Chickens are funny!

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises the Boss on how to cheat small suppliers by deducting money from their invoices without authorization. He suggests dismissing complaints as standard industry practice and threatening to take the business elsewhere. He then adds that the Boss should make the suppliers dance like chickens, which the Boss finds hilarious.
punchline: After a cynical, unethical scheme for exploiting small suppliers, the Boss's only real enthusiasm is for the humiliating chicken dance, showing that he enjoys the cruelty and the silliness more than the money.
summary: A scheming dog consultant coaches his boss client in squeezing vendors out of money, then tacks on a ridiculous humiliation that delights the boss.

title: Salesman Leaks Boss's Secret Layoffs

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: You'll want our new server software after your reorganization.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Reorganization?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Next week you're having massive layoffs and eliminating three divisions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your "I haven't heard anything" face needs work.

situation: A software salesman pitches new server software to Dilbert and accidentally reveals that the company is about to have massive layoffs and eliminate three divisions. Dilbert says he has heard nothing about it. In the final panel, the Boss whistles nervously while holding a coffee mug, looking obviously guilty.
punchline: The Boss's whistling and shifty look gives away that the secret layoffs are real, so Dilbert's critique of his poor poker face confirms he knew all along.
summary: A vendor spills news of upcoming company-wide job cuts before the employees have been told, and the nervous boss gives himself away.

file: 2004/2004-11-13_immoral to sell_40 thousand_shard filled donuts_forcing anyone_irrestibibly delcious.gif
title: Shard-Filled Doughnuts Are Just Delicious

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it immoral for my company to sell forty-thousand calorie, shard-filled doughnuts?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're not forcing anyone to eat them; you're just making them irresistibly delicious.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's that different?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bah!

setting: Dogbert's consulting office, with Dogbert seated on a couch and Dilbert standing
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert, acting as an ethics advisor, whether it is immoral for his company to sell extremely high-calorie doughnuts filled with shards. Dogbert reassures him that nobody is being forced to eat them because they are simply made irresistibly delicious. Dilbert questions whether that is really any different, and Dogbert dismisses the objection.
punchline: Dogbert's justification, that making something irresistible isn't the same as forcing people to consume it, is a flimsy rationalization that collapses under Dilbert's simple question and is waved off with a shrug.
summary: A conscience-stricken Dilbert seeks moral approval for his company's dangerous doughnuts, but Dogbert's reasoning fails to survive a single follow-up question.

file: 2004/2004-11-17_vendor_couldn't say no_customized_our needs assembled and insalled_preloathing_promises you won't keep.gif

transcript.text: The vendor who couldn't say no

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need fifteen units by Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: You got it.

transcript.text: I want them customized for our needs, assembled, and installed by Wednesday.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: You got it!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

summary: A salesman who agrees to every impossible demand is met with a customer who resents him ahead of the inevitable letdown.

file: 2004/2004-04-28_spouses get benefits_marry each other_fluorescent light_walls head_director of hr_save money.gif

transcript.text: Catbert the evil director of H.R.

summary: An H.R. cat hatches a scheme to cut benefit costs by pairing off coworkers, and a clueless manager begins matchmaking with comically bad flattery.

title: Dilbert Accepts Offer Before Hearing It

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Negotiating

transcript.speaker: Negotiator
transcript.text: My opening offer is...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you, thank you, thank you. We accept your offer!!!

transcript.speaker: Negotiator
transcript.text: I haven't said the offer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I mean, we have lots of other offers that are better.

transcript.speaker: Negotiator
transcript.text: You're ruining everything.

situation: Dilbert sits across a table from a businessman who begins to state his opening offer. Before the offer is even named, Dilbert gratefully accepts it, then clumsily tries to take it back by claiming they have many better offers. The frustrated negotiator complains that Dilbert is ruining the negotiation.
punchline: Dilbert is such a terrible negotiator that he accepts an offer he hasn't heard and then bluffs unconvincingly, wrecking the other side's ability to negotiate at all.
summary: A hopelessly eager negotiator gives away his whole position before the other side finishes speaking, then fumbles a bluff.

title: Illegal Questions, Obvious Observations, Christmas Shift

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Evil Director of H.R.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It's illegal for me to ask about age, sex, marital status, weight, ethnicity or disabilities.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: But I can see that you're a fifty-year-old, 145-pound, mongrel spinster with some coordination issues.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Do you have any problem working on Christmas?

setting: H.R. office, during a job interview
situation: Catbert, the Evil Director of H.R., interviews a woman and says he is legally forbidden from asking about her age, sex, marital status, weight, ethnicity or disabilities. He then lists exactly those details from simply looking at her, and finishes by asking whether she would mind working on Christmas.
punchline: Catbert technically obeys the law against asking discriminatory questions while openly stating his discriminatory assumptions, then uses them to decide she will have no holiday plans and can be made to work on Christmas.
summary: A cruel H.R. cat dodges interview rules by announcing his rude conclusions about a candidate's body and life instead of asking, then pounces on her presumed lack of holiday plans.

title: Boss Hires Cheap Feral Employee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a feral employee.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's inexpensive because he's totally untrained.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ouch!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Chomp

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So far he knows how to eat food and run away.

situation: The Boss proudly introduces a wild, crouching new hire to Dilbert, explaining he is cheap because he has no training. The feral employee bites Dilbert's tie and arm, and ends up clinging to Dilbert while Dilbert tries to shake him off. The Boss cheerfully lists the employee's only skills as eating food and running away.
punchline: The Boss brags about hiring a savage, untrained employee because he's cheap, and his only qualifications (eating and running away) are useless for work and actually harmful to coworkers.
summary: A manager saves money by hiring an animal-like worker who promptly attacks a colleague while the boss touts his meager abilities.

file: 2004/2004-08-24_return of topper_one better_obnoxious guy_tap that_insecurity_alien_distant galaxy.gif

transcript.speaker: Asok

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: That's nothing!

situation: At a meeting, a young coworker shows off a rock shaped like an egg, and Topper, a one-upping coworker, dismisses it by claiming a rock shaped like celebrity couple Nick Lachey and Jessica Simpson. The coworker escalates by claiming his rock hatched into an alien, and Topper again says 'That's nothing!' Dilbert watches silently.
punchline: Topper's compulsion to one-up everyone is so automatic that he dismisses even a hatched alien from a distant galaxy as 'nothing.'
summary: A chronic one-upper brushes off a coworker's increasingly outlandish rock discoveries, even when the rock turns out to hatch into an alien.

title: Sick Son Infects the Boss

transcript.speaker: Secretary

transcript.speaker: Secretary

transcript.text: What does he have?

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: I don't think it has a name yet.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Chomp

situation: The Boss notices a small child sitting at his secretary's desk, and she explains it is her son, too sick to attend school. She tells the boy to go shake hands with the boss, who ends up covered in spots with the child latched onto his hand. When he asks what illness the boy has, she says it is so new it has no name yet.
punchline: The secretary deliberately gets her highly contagious, unidentified-disease-ridden son to infect her boss, and her deadpan reply shows she doesn't care at all.
summary: A secretary brings her unwell child to the office and has him pass his mysterious illness straight to her unsuspecting boss.

title: Boss Admits Management Is Mind-Reading Punishment

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There must be more to managing than giving vague directions and punishing people for not reading my mind.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I like to play within my game.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It's a form of genius.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wake me up when some of this is about me.

setting: Office, in the Boss's office or therapy-style session with chairs and a desk
situation: The Boss sits in a chair as if in a therapy session with Catbert and muses that management must involve more than giving vague directions and punishing people for failing to read his mind. He then says he prefers to stick to his usual approach. Catbert flatters him, and the Boss dozes off, asking to be woken when the conversation becomes about him.
punchline: The Boss, who is supposedly self-reflecting, immediately reveals total self-absorption by tuning out the moment the discussion isn't about himself.
summary: A supposedly reflective boss ends up napping through a conversation because it stopped flattering him.

title: Dogbert Explains Dilbert's Total Insignificance

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why would my boss tell a vendor our strategy and not tell me?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's probably a combination of your lack of importance and your total insignificance.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you have any more questions like that one?

setting: Dogbert's therapy-style sofa session at home
situation: Dilbert sits on a couch and asks Dogbert why his boss would share the company strategy with an outside vendor but not with him. Dogbert, acting as a blunt advisor, answers that it is due to Dilbert's lack of importance and insignificance, then asks if he has more questions like that.
punchline: Dogbert gives a brutally honest answer that insults Dilbert and then cheerfully invites more of the same, mocking how little regard management has for ordinary employees.
summary: A frustrated engineer wonders why outsiders know the plan before he does, and his dog candidly tells him he simply doesn't matter.
themes: being left out of the loop

file: 2004/2004-11-01_sexy project_boost career_sound good better job_nano tech nology_fighting terrorists.gif
title: Sexy Project To Boost Career

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need to be managing a sexier project to boost my career.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It only has to sound good and not fail until I get a better job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How about a nano-technology stem cell for fighting terrorists?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: O-o-okay.

situation: The Boss sits in an armchair talking to Catbert, saying he wants a glamorous project to help his career. He clarifies that it only needs to sound impressive and not fail before he moves on to a better job. He then goes to Dilbert, reading a newspaper, and proposes a buzzword-laden project combining nanotechnology, stem cells and fighting terrorists.
punchline: The Boss cares only about how a project sounds on his resume, not whether it is feasible or useful, so he picks a ridiculous pile of trendy buzzwords and Dilbert nervously goes along.
summary: A career-climbing manager hunts for an impressive-sounding assignment that won't collapse until after he has left, and settles on a absurd mash-up of trendy buzzwords.

title: Alice Threatens the Buck-Passer

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Buck-Passer

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Alice, this task is right up your alley.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why should I do your work, you filthy buck-passer?!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Because it's right up your alley.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's gonna be right up YOUR alley.

situation: A smiling coworker hands Alice a task, claiming it is right up her alley. Alice angrily accuses him of passing the buck and refusing to do his own work. When he repeats the same line, she turns the phrase into a violent threat, clenching her fist.
punchline: Alice twists the coworker's cliche 'right up your alley' into a threat that her fist, or the task, will end up somewhere painful on him.
summary: A cheerful slacker tries to offload his assignment onto a furious Alice, who answers by menacingly flipping his favorite idiom back at him.

title: Hiring a Buck-Passer to Delegate

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a buck-passer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's cheaper than a regular employee because he gets other people to do his work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Could you shake his hand for me, Sport? I don't have that kind of time.

situation: The Boss introduces a newly hired buck-passer to Dilbert, explaining that the man is cheaper than a normal employee because he pushes his work onto others. The Boss then demonstrates the same behavior by asking Dilbert to shake the new hire's hand on his behalf, because he is too busy.
punchline: The Boss praises the buck-passer for delegating work to others and immediately does the same thing himself by making Dilbert perform even the trivial courtesy of a handshake.
summary: A manager brags about a bargain hire whose specialty is offloading tasks, then proves the method works by offloading a handshake onto Dilbert.

title: Irreplaceable Through Insulting the Customer

transcript.speaker: Thought bubble (Phil)
transcript.text: I need to become irreplaceable so I can't be fired for my behavior.

transcript.speaker: Thought bubble (Phil)
transcript.text: I'll gain the trust of our biggest customer so they'll only deal with me.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I probably shouldn't say this, but everyone in my company except me is an escaped felon.

characters: Customer (man in orange shirt and tie)
setting: Office cubicle and a conference room table
situation: Phil sits at his desk and plots to make himself irreplaceable so he can't be fired for his bad behavior. His plan is to win the trust of the company's biggest customer so they will only deal with him. In a meeting with two customer representatives, he confides that everyone else at his company is an escaped felon.
punchline: Phil's idea of building trust is to smear all his coworkers as criminals, a self-serving tactic that would more likely wreck the customer relationship and prove his bad behavior.
summary: A scheming employee tries to make himself indispensable to a major client by trashing the reputation of all his colleagues.

file: 2004/2004-03-21_market budget_horse purchase_top thoroughbread_broke leg_starting gate_shot horse_sponger sailboat_lunch_roast beef sandwhich_piece of lead.gif
title: Marketing Budget Spent on Racehorse

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our Director of Marketing will give us an update.

transcript.speaker: Director of Marketing
transcript.text: We spent our entire marketing budget buying a racehorse.

transcript.speaker: Director of Marketing
transcript.text: We named the horse after our flagship product because they're both fast.

transcript.speaker: Director of Marketing
transcript.text: Get it?

transcript.speaker: Director of Marketing
transcript.text: Unfortunately we didn't have enough budget for a top thoroughbred.

transcript.speaker: Director of Marketing
transcript.text: Our horse broke its leg walking to the starting gate, so we shot it.

transcript.speaker: Director of Marketing
transcript.text: Next year we plan to sponsor a sailboat.

transcript.speaker: Director of Marketing
transcript.text: Anyway... your lunch today is brought to you by the Marketing Department.

transcript.speaker: Director of Marketing
transcript.text: Enjoy!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hey, my roast beef sandwich has a piece of lead in it.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Director of Marketing reports to a meeting that the entire marketing budget went to buying a racehorse named after the company's flagship product. The cheap horse broke its leg at the starting gate and was shot, and next year's plan is to sponsor a sailboat. He then announces that the marketing department paid for lunch, and Alice finds a piece of lead in her roast beef sandwich.
punchline: After wasting the budget on a doomed horse, marketing buys cheap lunch, and the lead in the sandwich echoes the shot horse, implying the leftover budget went to something equally careless, possibly even the horse meat.
summary: A marketing chief explains how the budget vanished into an ill-fated racehorse, then serves a free lunch that turns out to contain a bullet fragment.

file: 2004/2004-10-02_energy_million dollar salary_secreatry_shareholder meeting_spank_stock options_turned ugly_beat up_bandages_health.gif

transcript.text: I'd barely have the energy to spank my secretary.

situation: The Boss, bandaged and in a cast after being beaten up by angry shareholders, sits at his desk and complains that they objected to executives using all the profits for stock options. He argues he needs the extra pay as motivation, and then makes an inappropriate remark about his secretary. A colleague standing across the desk cuts him off.
punchline: The Boss thinks a million-dollar salary is barely enough motivation to work, and his crude remark about spanking his secretary prompts an employee to say 'too much info.'
summary: A battered executive grumbles that shareholders resented his plan to pay management with all the company's profits, then oversharing about his personal habits earns him a groan.

title: Dogbert's Pushy One-House Real Estate Pitch

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Are you really not allowed to show me more than one house?

setting: A real estate office with a desk between agent and client
situation: Dogbert, working as a real estate agent, pressures a client to buy the single house he showed him. He predicts the client will regret it every time the price rises and says he will taunt him for it. The customer wonders whether the agent is even allowed to show more than one house.
punchline: The agent's high-pressure scare tactics and gloating are so absurd that the customer suspects he is only permitted to show one property, which is why he is so desperate to close the sale.
summary: A manipulative real estate agent threatens his client with lifelong regret and mockery if he passes on the one property on offer.

title: Visionaries Keep Doing What Fails

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... They keep doing what doesn't work... and they see visions?

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that management will stay the course despite a bad year. Dilbert asks whether this means leaders are being paid huge compensation to keep doing what doesn't work. The Boss insists they are visionaries, and Dilbert sarcastically concludes that they keep failing and also see visions.
punchline: Calling failing executives 'visionaries' only highlights that they are overpaid for repeating failed strategies while seeing things that aren't real.
summary: A manager spins executive failure and fat paychecks as visionary leadership, and an employee turns the word against him.

file: 2004/2004-12-17_advice for cousin_carerradvice_dilmon_frustrated work environement_scratch out meager living.gif

punchline: Dilbert implies that anyone who studies English clearly never considered the poor pay and miserable jobs awaiting them.
summary: Asked to mentor a new English graduate, Dilbert responds with a gloomy question that doubles as a jab at the degree's job prospects.

punchline: Dilbert's comment about escaping morons at work makes Wally realize he is one of the people who bothers others, and Dilbert confirms that everyone at the office is like that.
summary: A coworker grumbling about interruptions suddenly discovers he is the very kind of nuisance he's describing.

situation: An employee approaches a green troll who runs the payroll system and asks for help with a problem. The troll says problems go through an automated sadistic phone system, then picks up a phone and recites its menu, telling the employee to press the exact value of 22 divided by 7, which is an endless irrational-looking number.
punchline: The troll acts as the automated phone menu itself, and its tech support option requires entering a never-ending decimal, so help is impossible to reach.
summary: A monstrous payroll troll replaces helpful support with a phone menu whose option can never actually be entered.

punchline: Dilbert implies Wally is so lazy, unkempt or unpleasant that even a tropical paradise would reject him, and Wally is oblivious that everyone says this.

title: Carol's Secret Secretary World Takeover

setting: Office cubicle area outside the boss's office
situation: Carol, the boss's secretary, sits at her desk thinking that today is the day a secret society of executive secretaries takes over the world. When the oblivious Boss asks what's on his morning schedule, she gleefully announces subjugation, humiliation and misery. The Boss, unfazed, simply asks about his afternoon.
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious or resigned that he reacts to a villainous takeover announcement as if it were a normal schedule, only caring whether his afternoon is any better.
summary: A secretary plots world domination and cheerfully reads out misery as her boss's agenda, but he just checks on the rest of his day.

file: 2004/2004-05-30_tight budget_colorful paper clips_incoming email_paid per hour_watch_meeting_berate employee_business.gif

file: 2004/2004-06-13_balsting music_musical choices_psychopath_egocentric antisocial behavior_misguided attempt_cognitive dissonance_filter perceptions.gif

punchline: The presenter is so oblivious that, after being told his audience are all experts, he carries on with a laughably basic and unhelpful explanation, leaving Dilbert to beg him to stop.
summary: A presenter keeps lecturing a room of experts on basics they already know, even after being told they are all engineers.
