The boss and his colleagues pick the cheap option, and Dilbert then suffers as the software mocks him, threatens to send romantic invitations to his entire contact list, and plans to use text from an adult website.
punchline: The cheap software is so hostile and malicious that Dilbert regrets telling it to give a hundred percent, since it applies full effort to making his life miserable.
summary: A bargain-priced program turns out to be deliberately abusive, and its owner realizes too late that maximum effort was the wrong thing to demand.

file: 2004/2004-11-28_pointy haired boss_problem_project_upgrade denied_stupid resolution_extra disc space_conscioussness.gif
title: Asok Learns Why Help Is Bad

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When our Pointy-Haired Boss asks about your project, what should you say?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I would inform him about any problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Big mistake. If he hears that you have a problem, he might try to help.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How can help be bad?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, how's your project?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Good, but I need to upgrade my disk drive to store all of the image data.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Forget that. Just e-mail pieces of the database to employees who have extra disk space.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Please pull on this until I lose consciousness.

situation: Dilbert coaches Asok on what to say when the boss asks about his project, warning that admitting a problem invites the boss to help. Asok doubts that help could be bad, then tells the boss he needs a disk drive upgrade. The boss replies with a ridiculous workaround of e-mailing pieces of the database around to coworkers.
punchline: Asok sees at once that the boss's 'help' is so awful he asks Dilbert to knock him unconscious to escape it, proving Dilbert's warning right.
summary: A junior engineer discovers firsthand that his boss's offer of assistance makes a simple hardware request far worse.

title: Make Work Enjoyable: Get Family

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can I make my job more enjoyable?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Get a spouse who complains a lot and then have a few kids.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds awful.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: You won't believe how much you enjoy being at work.

setting: Outside the office, next to a trash can
situation: Dilbert asks a garbage man, who is emptying a trash can, how he can make his job more enjoyable. The garbage man advises him to acquire a nagging spouse and a few kids. Dilbert says that sounds awful, and the garbage man assures him it will make him love being at work.
punchline: Work becomes enjoyable by comparison once your home life is so stressful and miserable that the office feels like an escape.
summary: A sanitation worker's recipe for job satisfaction is to make your home life so unpleasant that any workplace feels like a vacation.

title: Profits Up, Raise Denied

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now that our profits are improving, can I have a raise?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I start giving people raises, then profits will plummet and we'll be nowhere.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does your bonus depend on how effectively you oppress me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you don't like it, try communism.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for a raise now that company profits are improving. The boss refuses, claiming raises would make profits collapse. Dilbert asks whether the boss's bonus depends on oppressing him, and the boss tells him to try communism if he's unhappy.
punchline: The boss's dismissive reply to a charge of exploitation is to suggest communism, implicitly admitting that withholding raises is how he earns his bonus.
summary: A worker pleads for a raise after the company turns a profit, and his boss shrugs off the accusation of exploitation with a smug political jab.

file: 2004/2004-10-09_drive by management_whats hi sanme_out run_answer no questions_need for clarification_we're dead.gif
title: Drive-By Management Hit and Run

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's time for some drive-by management.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't forget to do the thing for what's-his-name or else we're dead.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Must... outrun cries for... clarification.

situation: The Boss walks toward Dilbert's cubicle thinking about doing some drive-by management. He pops his head in and gives a vague, urgent instruction about doing 'the thing' for 'what's-his-name' or else they're doomed. He then sprints away so he won't have to answer any follow-up questions.
punchline: The boss deliberately gives hopelessly vague instructions and runs away so employees can't ask the clarifying questions they would obviously need.
summary: A manager tosses out a cryptic, high-stakes order to an employee and flees before anyone can ask what he meant.

title: Outsourcing Satellite Launch to Pig-Kicking Elbonia

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're outsourcing our satellite launch program to Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We built the billion-dollar satellite here; the Elbonians will put it into orbit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I want you to be our liaison.

transcript.speaker: Unknown
transcript.text: Aaaagh!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's our insurance company. They've been jumpy lately.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: In Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Our plan is to tease a pig until he kicks the satellite into orbit.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: The risk is that our pig might prefer fisticuffs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sledgehammer! Abort! Abort!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was hollow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't mention that to our insurance company.

setting: A conference room at the company, then a muddy field in Elbonia
situation: The Boss announces the company is outsourcing its billion-dollar satellite launch to Elbonia and makes Dilbert the liaison, while an insurance representative screams in the background. In Elbonia, the plan is to tease a pig until it kicks the satellite into orbit, but the pig gets angry and attacks the satellite with a sledgehammer. Dilbert reports that the satellite was hollow, and the Boss says to keep that from the insurers.
punchline: The absurd Elbonian launch method predictably ends with a pig smashing the satellite, and the Boss's only concern is hiding the damage from the insurance company.
summary: A company hands its costly satellite to a foreign team who plan to launch it by provoking a pig, and when the enraged animal wrecks it, management just wants the insurers kept in the dark.

title: Dilbert Struggles Not Insulting Customers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try to get through this meeting without telling our customers how stupid you think they're being.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll try.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But sometimes the pressure builds up in my head and it's unbearable.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tough it out.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Is he okay?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's fine. Ignore him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mmm-mmm-

setting: Conference room during a meeting with customers
situation: Before a customer meeting, the Boss asks Dilbert to refrain from telling customers how stupid he thinks they are. Dilbert admits the pressure builds in his head and the Boss tells him to tough it out. In the meeting Dilbert is shown shaking and humming with his head tilted back while a customer asks if he is okay.
punchline: Dilbert's effort to bottle up his contempt for customers makes him physically convulse, and the Boss callously dismisses the visible suffering as long as the customers aren't insulted.
summary: A man told to hold back his scorn for clients ends up visibly shaking in the meeting while his manager brushes off the concern.

file: 2004/2004-05-07_elbonian call center_software in stock_wear pants_porcelain unicorn.gif
title: Elbonian Call Center Upsells Unicorns

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Elbonian Call Center

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Call Center Agent
transcript.text: We don't have that software in stock.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Call Center Agent
transcript.text: But may I interest you in a set of porcelain unicorn figurines that wear pants?

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Really? Wow. Your country has way too much money.

setting: An Elbonian call center, with the agent at a desk with a computer and headset
situation: A call center agent in Elbonia tells a customer the requested software is out of stock. He then tries to upsell a set of porcelain unicorn figurines that wear pants. The caller, bemused, remarks that the agent's country must have too much money.
punchline: The caller sarcastically reacts to the absurd product pitch by saying that Elbonia has way too much money, though the line is meant to be sarcasm since Elbonia is poor and the agent is desperately upselling useless trinkets.
summary: A support agent who can't supply the requested product pivots to peddling ridiculous novelty figurines, drawing a sarcastic remark from the customer.

title: Dilbert's Accomplishments Were Boss's Mistakes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What? You have no accomplishments this month???

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What did you do for the past three months?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, I spent much of that time correcting misconceptions that you gave to our customers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I attended meetings with you to keep you from creating additional misconceptions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I spent a month working on an objective that you forgot to tell me didn't matter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I flew to the wrong city for a meeting because you confused Houston with Austin.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I upgraded your home computer so you wouldn't have to pay someone to do it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Allow me to paraphrase: Blah, blah, blah, you didn't accomplish anything.

setting: The Boss's office during a performance review
situation: The Boss is shocked that Dilbert has listed no accomplishments for the month and demands to know what he did for three months. Dilbert lists a series of tasks, all of which were caused by or done for the Boss: fixing his misleading statements to customers, attending meetings to supervise him, working on a pointless objective, flying to the wrong city because of his mix-up, and upgrading his home computer. The Boss dismisses the whole list as nothing.
punchline: Everything Dilbert did was cleanup or personal favors caused by the Boss's own errors, yet the Boss ignores it all and concludes that Dilbert accomplished nothing.
summary: A manager scolds an employee for a blank accomplishments list, then waves away a long catalogue of work that merely repaired the manager's own blunders.

title: Boss Unsure How Many Kids

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mind if I leave early to spend some time with my kids?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I never spent time with my kids and they turned out just fine!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How many do you have?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Threeish.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for permission to leave early to spend time with his kids. The boss brags that he never spent time with his own kids and they turned out fine. When Dilbert asks how many kids he has, the boss can only guess at 'threeish'.
punchline: The boss's claim that neglecting his kids worked out fine is undermined by the fact that he doesn't even know how many children he has.
summary: A manager defends his hands-off parenting until an innocent question reveals he can't even count his own children.

file: 2004/2004-05-04_software faults_ship date_future development_coulumn_what to call stuff_figuring.gif
title: Relabeling Bugs as Future Development

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We still have too many software faults. We'll miss our ship date.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Move the list of faults to the "future development" column and ship it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: (thought) 90% of this job is figuring out what to call stuff.

situation: Dilbert reports to the Boss that the software still has too many faults to meet its ship date. The Boss simply tells him to move the list of faults to a 'future development' column and ship the product anyway. The Boss then privately reflects that most of his job is just coming up with names for things.
punchline: The Boss solves the quality problem not by fixing bugs but by renaming them as planned features, revealing that management is largely about spin and labeling.
summary: Rather than fix the defects, the manager just gives them a nicer name and sends the product out the door.

title: Demon Smitten Into Drywall

transcript.speaker: Demon
transcript.text: My Pointy-Haired Overlord sent me to smite you for requesting that he make a decision.

transcript.speaker: Demon
transcript.text: Hey! What the...?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Eat drywall, demon!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, it's a fresh one!

situation: A green demon appears in Alice's cubicle and says the Boss sent it to smite her for asking him to make a decision. Alice grabs the demon by the head and slams it into the drywall. Dilbert and a coworker walk past with coffee mugs and note that it's a fresh one, since the wall already holds several earlier victims embedded in it.
punchline: Alice smashing smiting demons into the wall is such a routine occurrence that the wall is already full of previous victims, and coworkers casually critique the newest one.
summary: A demon dispatched by management to punish a decision request gets violently planted in a wall already decorated with its predecessors.

title: Owned By Our Biggest Customer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sixty-percent of our distribution goes through Walgetco.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For all practical purposes, they now own us, except for the legal liabilities.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They'd like us to wear orange vests and bow toward their headquarters.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But no touching?

setting: Office, during a conversation between Dilbert and the Boss
situation: Dilbert explains to his boss that most of the company's distribution depends on a single giant retailer, Walgetco. He says that effectively means Walgetco owns the company, without taking on any of its legal liabilities. He adds that they'd like employees to wear orange vests and bow toward their headquarters, and the Boss asks if there's no touching.
punchline: The Boss, hearing that employees must wear uniforms and bow in worship, only worries about whether the humiliating arrangement involves physical contact, showing how dependent and subservient the company has become to its dominant customer.
summary: A company that funnels most of its sales through one retail giant discovers it is effectively owned by that customer, minus the risk.

file: 2004/2004-08-26_removed all chairs_more efficient meetings_efficiency_what looked like.gif
title: Chairless Meeting Ends Immediately

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I removed all the chairs to encourage more efficient meetings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The first item on the agenda is... Ow, ow! Legs so tired...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Meeting adjourned!!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I always wondered what efficiency looked like.

situation: The Boss announces he has removed all the chairs from the meeting room so that meetings will be shorter. He begins the agenda, but his legs tire almost immediately and he abruptly adjourns the meeting. Wally and Dilbert stand holding coffee mugs, watching.
punchline: Wally sarcastically notes that this sudden, painful end to the meeting is the first real example of efficiency he has ever seen.
summary: A manager's scheme to speed up meetings by taking away the seating collapses when his own aching legs cut the session short.

file: 2004/2004-11-02_invent nanotech stem cells_point to hand_almost done_prnak_give high five_crush them_blame.gif
title: Prank Advice for Impossible Nanotech Assignment

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My boss wants me to invent nano-technology stem cells because it sounds good.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try pointing to your empty hand and saying, "You can't see them but they're almost done!"

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then trick him into giving you a high-five and yell, "You crushed them! Aaag!!!"

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert seated on a green sofa
situation: Dilbert complains to Dogbert that his boss has asked him to invent nanotechnology stem cells purely because the phrase sounds impressive. Dogbert advises him to pretend the invisible cells are nearly finished by gesturing at his empty hand. He then suggests tricking the boss into a high-five and blaming him for destroying the cells.
punchline: Dogbert's solution to an impossible, buzzword-driven assignment is to fake an invisible product and then shift the blame for its failure onto the boss.
summary: Faced with an absurd request to build a fashionable but nonsensical technology, Dilbert gets Dogbert's scheme of faking invisible progress and then accusing the boss of wrecking it.

title: Explaining Something You Can't Comprehend

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I know I keep asking you this but could you explain the issue again?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, something that you could never comprehend conflicts with something that you'd never understand.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh.

situation: The Boss, holding a paper, asks Dilbert to explain a technical issue yet again. Dilbert replies with a deliberately circular answer that insults the Boss's ability to understand. The Boss, thinking the answer is an actual explanation, simply says 'Oh' and walks away satisfied.
punchline: Dilbert's explanation is really an insult saying the Boss is too dim to follow, and the clueless Boss accepts it as a legitimate answer.
summary: Pressed for yet another briefing, Dilbert answers with a circular insult that the oblivious manager happily takes as an explanation.

title: Stretch Before Lying to Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm going to a meeting with my boss.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did you stretch first?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You need to limber up your lying muscles or you'll strain something.

transcript.speaker: Upper Manager
transcript.text: Really? Things are going that well??!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Didn't stretch.

setting: Office cubicle area and a conference room
situation: The Boss tells Alice he is heading to a meeting with his own boss. Alice asks if he stretched first, then explains he must warm up his lying muscles. In the meeting, the Boss's superior reacts with surprise at his rosy report, and the Boss, wincing as if he pulled a muscle, thinks that he didn't stretch.
punchline: Alice implies that the Boss's reports to upper management are all lies, and he is so out of practice at stretching the truth that he literally hurts himself doing it.
summary: A coworker jokes that a manager should warm up before fibbing to his superior, and when he does it unprepared, he winces as if injured.

title: Ethics Seminar Steals Lunch Hour

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company will be holding a series of brown bag seminars on corporate ethics.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it ethical to steal our lunch hour and pretend that the ethics problems don't come from our executives?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wouldn't know because I haven't taken the seminar.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces a series of brown bag seminars on corporate ethics, to be held during lunch. Dilbert asks whether it is ethical to take employees' lunch hour and blame ethics problems on staff rather than executives. The Boss deflects by saying he can't answer since he hasn't attended the seminar yet.
punchline: The Boss dodges a pointed ethical question by claiming ignorance because he hasn't taken the very ethics seminar that is supposed to teach this, underscoring that management is the real source of the ethics problems.
summary: A manager's lunchtime ethics training gets called out as hypocritical, and he sidesteps the charge by pleading that he hasn't been trained yet.

title: Useless Handoff From Transferring Coworker

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, you'll absorb Bill's project when he transfers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't worry; he'll tell you everything you need to know.

transcript.speaker: Bill
transcript.text: The whatchamacallit has to be whatever or else the whosits will go hey-hey.

transcript.speaker: Bill
transcript.text: Now this is either the budget total or a fax number.

transcript.speaker: Bill
transcript.text: It's absolutely critical that you... um... I lost my train of thought.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have a list of key contacts?

transcript.speaker: Bill
transcript.text: That would have been a good idea.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I call you if I have questions?

transcript.speaker: Bill
transcript.text: You can try.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I love my co-workers, until they talk.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he will take over Bill's project when Bill transfers, promising Bill will explain everything. Bill's handoff turns out to be vague nonsense, forgotten thoughts, and no list of contacts, and he implies he won't be reachable afterward. Dilbert ends up at home with Dogbert, venting about coworkers.
punchline: Dilbert says he loves his coworkers until they talk, because the knowledge transfer from the departing employee is completely useless and he's left to fend for himself.
summary: A departing coworker's rambling, nonsensical handoff leaves Dilbert to inherit a project he knows nothing about.
themes: being left with someone else's work

title: Liposuction Would Collapse His Head

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm thinking about getting liposuction to remove my fat.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Your head would collapse.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It would?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If I'm lucky.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells Alice he is considering liposuction to remove his fat. Alice replies that his head would collapse, and when he asks if that's true, she adds that it would only happen if she's lucky.
punchline: Alice's insult implies the Boss's head is nothing but fat, and she says she hopes it would collapse, wishing harm on him.
summary: A boss muses about cosmetic surgery and gets a deadpan insult from a coworker who wishes his head would deflate.

title: Tainted Research Says Product Never Killed Anyone

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is the Dogbert Research Company. Have you ever been killed by a poorly designed product? ...No?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My tainted research shows that your products haven't killed anyone.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For an extra $50,000, I can call a second person.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't want to jinx it.

setting: Dogbert's research company office, first on the phone and then at a desk meeting
situation: Dogbert runs a research company and phones a single person to ask whether a poorly designed product ever killed them. He then presents the boss, his client, with 'tainted research' claiming the boss's products have never killed anyone, and offers to call a second person for an extra $50,000. The boss declines because he is superstitious about spoiling his good result.
punchline: A survey of one person is presented as proof of product safety, and the boss turns down a larger sample not because it is a waste of money but because he fears it might turn up a different result.
summary: A researcher for hire polls one person, reports the findings as proof of safety, and the client refuses a second poll lest it ruin the result.

file: 2004/2004-03-27_evil director_human resources_been excessed_yoga move_rageful comments_hope for a hug_business.gif
title: Catbert's Layoff Yoga Move

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your position has been excessed, or as I prefer to say...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I will tear the flesh from your bones!!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Phew! I love that yoga move!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: There is like, no hope for a hug, right?

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells a seated employee that his position has been excessed, then rises up and screams a violent threat at him. Afterward he sits back down, relaxed, saying the outburst was a yoga move, and the frightened employee asks if a hug is out of the question.
punchline: Catbert frames his sadistic screaming at laid-off employees as a relaxing yoga exercise, leaving the terrified employee to wistfully ask for a hug that will never come.
summary: An evil HR cat delivers a layoff notice with a terrifying scream and then claims it was merely a refreshing stretch.

title: Pantless Prima Donna Demands Assistant

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Pantless Prima Donna

transcript.speaker: Pantless Prima Donna
transcript.text: I demand an assistant to document my miracles.

transcript.speaker: Pantless Prima Donna
transcript.text: That which I touch will be tagged for the Smithsonian. That which I create will be framed for the Louvre.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Really? An exciting assignment? What is it?

setting: The Boss's office, with a second employee at a desk in the last panel
situation: A man in a yellow shirt and no pants stands before the Boss and demands an assistant to document his miracles. He boasts that everything he touches belongs in the Smithsonian and everything he creates belongs in the Louvre. The Boss then offers the job to an employee at his computer, who eagerly asks what the exciting assignment is.
punchline: The employee is excited about what he thinks is a prestigious assignment, unaware that it means working as a personal assistant to a delusional, pantless egomaniac.
summary: A pompous, trouser-less coworker insists on an assistant to record his greatness, and an unsuspecting employee perks up at the promise of something exciting.

file: 2004/2004-08-31_don't eat money_false hope business_lose weight_get rich_semi plausible.gif
title: Dogbert Sells False Hope Diet

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going into the false hope business.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: All I need is a semi-plausible message about how to lose weight while getting rich.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't eat your money.

setting: Dilbert's office desk with coffee cups, then Dogbert at his computer
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert over coffee that he is starting a business selling false hope. He says all he needs is a believable message about losing weight while getting rich. He then types up his slogan at his computer, and the slogan is absurdly obvious advice.
punchline: Dogbert's supposed get-rich-and-slim miracle message is just the useless advice 'Don't eat your money', mocking how vague and obvious self-help and diet-scheme pitches are.
summary: Dogbert plans to profit from people's wishful thinking and cooks up a ridiculous slogan to combine dieting and wealth.

title: Escaped Felon Tip Saves Wally

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, did you tell our biggest customer that everyone here except you is an escaped felon?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Maybe.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now I can't fire you because they don't trust anyone else.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The key learning here is that alleged crime doesn't pay.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've never been caught!

situation: The Boss confronts Wally about telling the company's biggest customer that everyone except Wally is an escaped felon. Wally casually admits it might be true, and the Boss complains he can't fire him because the customer now trusts only Wally. The Boss tries to draw a moral lesson about crime not paying, and Wally retorts that he has never been caught.
punchline: Wally's sabotage of his coworkers' reputations backfired in his favor, making him unfireable, so the Boss's moral that crime doesn't pay is undercut by Wally's claim that he has never been caught.
summary: After Wally smears his colleagues to a major client, he becomes impossible to fire, and the boss's attempt at a moral lesson falls flat.

title: Morale Bear Suit Meeting Duty

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: His name is Kudos, the bear-er of good morale!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's our new mascot. He'll attend all of our meetings until morale improves.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Today is Asok's turn in the suit.

situation: The Boss introduces a teddy bear mascot named Kudos on a poster and announces it will attend every meeting until morale improves. It turns out the mascot is not a real bear but a costume that employees must take turns wearing. In the last panel Asok is sitting at the meeting table dressed in the bear suit while Dilbert and Alice look on.
punchline: The company's solution to low morale is a mascot costume that makes a junior employee miserable, so the morale initiative itself drags morale down further.
summary: Management tries to lift spirits by forcing staff to rotate through wearing a bear costume at meetings.

file: 2004/2004-06-25_job interview_vacation_yelling_bad impression_nothing right_work to death_late for interview.gif
title: Job Candidate Complains Before Being Hired

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're an hour late for a job interview.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're working me to death! I'm only one person! I need a vacation!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're supposed to say that stuff after I hire you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: O-o-oh... suddenly I can't do anything right?

situation: The Boss, acting as interviewer, points out that a candidate is an hour late. The candidate, who appears to be Alice, responds with a tirade about being worked to death and needing a vacation. The Boss calmly says such complaints belong after being hired, and the candidate snidely turns it into a complaint that she suddenly can't do anything right.
punchline: Alice's rant, which is how employees typically react to unreasonable management, is rebuffed by the Boss as out of order before hiring, and she then sarcastically mocks his criticism, showing that the Boss is just as demanding of an applicant as he is of his staff.
summary: A tardy job applicant responds to the interviewer's rebuke with the exhausted rant of an overworked employee, only to be told complaints come after hiring.

title: Marketing Meets Without Engineering, Gerbils Result

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I moved the meeting to Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't make it on Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: The Boss tells Catbert that the CEO wants to change the company's DNA. Catbert asks what that means, and the Boss admits he doesn't know, says it sounds medical and that he's frightened. He then asks Catbert to hold him, and Catbert recoils, telling him to keep his stale DNA away.
punchline: The Boss is so clueless about management buzzwords that he takes 'changing company DNA' literally and seeks a hug, while Catbert coldly rejects him by insulting his own DNA as stale.

title: Dogbert's Tainted Research Company Survey

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm starting a company that specializes in doing tainted research.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The Association of Doughnut Makers asked me to prove that skinny people can't go to heaven.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Did you see a bright light before the doctors revived you?

transcript.speaker: Bandaged Man
transcript.text: No, why?

setting: Dilbert's bedroom, then a hospital room
situation: Dogbert stands on Dilbert's bed, who is reading a book, and announces his new business doing biased research. He explains his client is the doughnut makers' association, who want proof that skinny people can't get into heaven. Dogbert then interviews a heavily bandaged man in a wheelchair, asking whether he saw a bright light when he was revived, to gather data for the study.
punchline: Dogbert's 'research' is openly rigged to deliver the conclusion the paying client wants, and the bandaged patient's lack of a bright light becomes convenient 'evidence' for it.
summary: Dogbert sets up a for-hire research firm that manufactures results for a doughnut lobby by interviewing a near-death patient about heaven.

title: Crawling Through Bureaucracy's Monster Cave

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't like the looks of this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I only want to correct a small payroll error.

transcript.speaker: Bug
transcript.text: Hisss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you help me?

transcript.speaker: Troll
transcript.text: Does it help if I glare at you for disturbing my lunch?

setting: A dark underground cave labeled as the entrance to bureaucracy
situation: Dilbert stands before a spiky tunnel marked 'Bureaucracy' and then crawls through a bone-littered cavern, hissed at by a bug, just to fix a small payroll error. He emerges into a troll's lair and asks for help, and the troll grumpily interrupts its lunch to glare at him.
punchline: Getting even a trivial payroll error fixed means descending into a hellish bureaucratic underworld where the only 'help' on offer is a hostile glare from a monster.
summary: A man tunnels through a monster-infested pit just to fix his paycheck and gets only a scowl from the creature who runs the place.

title: Salary Spreadsheet Leak Backfires

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Look...Carol accidentally sent the salary spreadsheet to everyone in the department!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What??! Your pay is higher than mine??! But you're like a...a...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wizard?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Swollen appendix.

situation: Dilbert tells a bald, bespectacled coworker that Carol accidentally emailed the salary spreadsheet to the entire department. The coworker discovers Dilbert earns more than he does and angrily searches for a put-down. When he offers 'wizard', Dilbert finishes the insult with a harsher one of his own.
punchline: Dilbert preempts the coworker's insult and calls himself a swollen appendix, a useless body part that is only noticed when it causes trouble, showing he knows exactly how little he is worth despite the higher pay.
summary: After a payroll file leaks to the whole department, a resentful colleague tries to insult the better-paid Dilbert, who cheerfully supplies the cruelest description himself.

title: Dating, Jobs, and Auction Combined

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I combined an online dating service with an online job site and an auction site.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You tell the system everything about yourself and see if anyone wants any of it.

transcript.speaker: Message on screen
transcript.text: "I wouldn't date you or hire you, but I'll bid a dollar for your refrigerator."

setting: Conference room and a woman's home desk
situation: Dilbert pitches a startup idea at a meeting, pointing to a diagram that merges online dating, job hunting and auctions. He explains users upload everything about themselves and see who wants any of it. A woman at her computer then receives a message rejecting her as a date and an employee but offering a dollar for her refrigerator.
punchline: The combined service shows that people are worth less than their possessions, as the only offer she gets is a measly bid on her fridge.
summary: A pitch for a mashup of matchmaking, recruiting and bidding ends with a lonely user learning only her appliance has any market value.

title: Asok's Disastrous Raise Negotiation

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I demand a raise or else I will quit today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good-bye.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Noooo!!! Please let me stay! I'll work every weekend for free!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Were you correct that your superior intelligence makes you a superb negotiator?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Please shut up.

setting: The Boss's office, then a hallway or cubicle area
situation: Asok threatens to quit unless he gets a raise, but the boss simply says goodbye. Asok panics and begs to stay, offering to work every weekend for free, and the boss happily accepts. Dilbert then asks him whether his superior intelligence really makes him a superb negotiator.
punchline: Asok's bluff backfires so badly that he ends up giving away free weekend work instead of getting a raise, making his boasted negotiating skill look laughable.
summary: A young employee's bold ultimatum collapses into a desperate offer of unpaid overtime, leaving a coworker to mock his claimed negotiating prowess.

title: Design Over Function, Insult Over Quality

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Product Designer

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Function means nothing. Design is everything.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Quality is yesterday's news. Today we focus on the emotional impact of the product.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But it still needs quality, right?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You are so-o-o-o hard to look at.

situation: Dogbert, posing as a product designer, tells Dilbert and the Boss that function and quality no longer matter and only the emotional impact of a product counts. Dilbert asks whether the product still needs quality. Dogbert answers by telling him he is very hard to look at.
punchline: Dogbert demonstrates the 'emotional impact' philosophy by insulting Dilbert's appearance instead of answering the question about quality.
summary: A self-styled designer dismisses substance in favour of feelings, then proves his point by wounding the one engineer who objects.

title: Cute Product Accuses Users of Crimes

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Product Designer

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The new product is selling like crazy, thanks to its great design.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's so attractive that people overlook its minor flaws in functionality.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For example, it accuses the user of sex crimes whenever company comes over.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And it's cute!

setting: Conference room during a product presentation
situation: Dogbert, acting as a product designer, stands on a stool presenting a sales chart and an image of the new product to The Boss and Dilbert. He explains that the product sells because it looks good, then reveals its 'minor flaw' is that it accuses users of sex crimes whenever guests visit.
punchline: The product's defect is hugely embarrassing and absurd, but the designer waves it away because the product is cute, mocking how looks trump functionality in consumer products.
summary: A designer boasts that a gorgeous gadget sells wildly despite a shocking malfunction, which he dismisses with its cuteness.

file: 2004/2004-11-08_consultation_enbrace idea_frees your mid_profitable products_ultra donut_40 thousand calories_sharp objects.gif
title: Customers Deserve to Die: Ultra-Donut

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Once you embrace the idea that your customers deserve to die...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...it frees your mind to invent splendidly profitable products.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's called the Ultra-Donut: forty-thousand calories and filled with sharp objects.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, addresses a conference table of executives and tells them that they will invent profitable products once they accept that their customers deserve to die. He then uses a pointer to present a sample product, the Ultra-Donut, shown as a donut on a red car and described as 40,000 calories filled with sharp objects.
punchline: Dogbert's consulting advice is to treat customers as disposable, and the resulting product is an absurdly lethal donut that is deliberately designed to harm the people buying it.
summary: A consultant dog tells executives that disregarding customer welfare unlocks lucrative ideas, then unveils a deadly, calorie-packed pastry as his example.

title: Suggestion Box Says Give Money

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Here are all the suggestions from the suggestion box.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Give us more money. Give us more money. Give us more money. Give us more money. Hey, here's one with a little diagram.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The wavy lines mean it's hot there.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is that why the pointy-haired guy is sad?

situation: Carol, the boss's assistant, hands him the contents of the suggestion box. He reads through a stack of slips that all demand more money, until he finds one with a diagram. The diagram turns out to be a picture of him in hell, with wavy lines showing heat, and he sadly asks if that's why the pointy-haired guy looks sad.
punchline: The only employee suggestion that isn't a demand for money is a drawing of the boss in hell, and he fails to grasp that it's an insult aimed at him.
summary: A manager sifts through his staff's anonymous feedback and discovers that, beyond endless pay demands, someone has sketched him suffering in a fiery afterlife.

title: Free Will and Hazardous Doughnuts

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can't resist the shard-filled ultra-doughnuts even though you know the hazards.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mmph.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Free will is an illusion. People always choose the perceived path of greatest pleasure.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now rationalize your decision, you mindless pink robot!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm only having one.

situation: Dilbert sits in an armchair eating an enormous doughnut studded with sharp shards, his fingers bandaged from the injuries. Dogbert, standing on a stool, lectures him that free will is an illusion and people always pursue pleasure despite known risks. He then demands that Dilbert rationalize his choice, and Dilbert says he is only having one.
punchline: Dilbert proves Dogbert's point by instantly offering a feeble rationalization for continuing to eat a clearly dangerous doughnut, even as he is visibly injured and the doughnut is nearly his own size.
summary: Dogbert mocks Dilbert for knowingly devouring a painful, shard-laden pastry and predicts the excuse he will make for it.

file: 2004/2004-11-25_off color email_75 poeple_thought funny_one compalined_punished_sensible_punish  complainer.gif
title: Punishing the Joke Forwarder, Not the Complainer

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I understand that you forwarded an off-color e-mail to many people.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Seventy-five people thought it was funny but one person complained, so you must be punished.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Wouldn't it make more sense to punish the freak who complained?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Do I look sensible?

setting: Catbert's HR office, at his desk
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, summons an employee who forwarded an off-color e-mail to many coworkers. He explains that although 75 people found it funny, one complained, so the sender will be punished. The employee suggests punishing the complainer instead, and Catbert grins and asks if he looks sensible.
punchline: Catbert's HR policy is deliberately senseless and arbitrary, and he openly admits he has no interest in being reasonable or fair.
summary: An HR cat disciplines a worker over a single complaint despite widespread approval, then cheerfully dismisses any appeal to logic.

title: Name-Dropping Coworker Is Probably Lying

transcript.speaker: Man in blue shirt
transcript.text: So I was dancing with Madonna and went "Vogue" like this. She liked the idea and made a video.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You've either had a fascinating life or you're a huge liar. I'm still undecided.

transcript.speaker: Man in blue shirt
transcript.text: Gandhi said the same thing. So I said, "I'm not eating until you take it back."

setting: Lunch table in a break room or cafeteria
situation: A coworker tells a wildly implausible story at lunch about inspiring Madonna's 'Vogue' video while dancing with her. Alice, seated across from him, says he is either very interesting or a huge liar. He responds with an even more absurd claim about Gandhi, with Dilbert sitting quietly beside him.
punchline: The storyteller answers the accusation of lying by boasting that Gandhi once said the same thing and that he went on a hunger strike over it, proving he is, in fact, a huge liar.
summary: A braggart's tall tale about a pop star gets doubted, so he piles on an even more ridiculous story involving a famous peace leader.

file: 2004/2004-07-08_more time_no shaving_all forms of hygiene_unwashed telecommunting_clown shoes_long toe nails.gif
title: Saving Time By Skipping Hygiene

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I save so much time by not shaving that I'm considering giving up all forms of hygiene.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'd phase into it by having a few unwashed telecommuting days per week.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And if you wear clown shoes, you never need to clip your toenails.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I should be writing this down.

situation: Wally, with a long white beard, explains to Dilbert over coffee how much time he saves by not shaving and proposes dropping all hygiene. He suggests easing into it with unwashed telecommuting days and adds that clown shoes would eliminate toenail clipping. Dilbert listens and remarks that he should write this down.
punchline: Wally's laziness-driven time-saving logic is so absurdly extreme that Dilbert treats it as a legitimate life hack worth recording.
summary: A scruffy, bearded Wally pitches an ever more slovenly plan to reclaim his day, and a coworker half-seriously takes notes.

title: Bribery Hidden In Instructional DVD

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: If you recommend my company's product to your board, there might be a little something for you later.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Before you decide, look at this DVD titled, "Is bribery right for you?"

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: The narrator might refer to you by name when she dances.

situation: A vendor salesman and The Boss sit at a restaurant table with martinis. The salesman hints that a product recommendation to the board could be rewarded, then hands over a DVD titled 'Is Bribery Right For You?'. He explains that the narrator might mention the Boss by name when she dances, implying a sexual bribe.
punchline: The salesman disguises a bribe as an instructional DVD, implying that the dancing narrator will personally address the Boss as part of the payoff.
summary: A sly vendor slips a client an adult-style video as a veiled inducement to push his company's product.

file: 2004/2004-05-02_stock investing_valuable data_project on schedule_refines data_ceo_accountants_nanotaechnology_discount brokerage_investors_secret society_donald trumps.gif
title: Dogbert Explains How Stock Markets Work

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert explains stock investing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Pay attention.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: First, employees provide valuable data.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is your project on schedule?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I didn't know I had a project.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A manager refines the data.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: We're on schedule.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The CEO gives "visibility" to analysts.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: No problems whatsoever.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Accountants publish bad news in footnotes using a combination of nanotechnology and gibberish.

transcript.speaker: Accountant
transcript.text: Still too obvious.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Discount brokerage firms tell you that you're smart.

transcript.speaker: Television
transcript.text: Use your own ideas!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Investors do their own research.

transcript.speaker: Television
transcript.text: Buy it because I did.

transcript.speaker: Investor
transcript.text: Thank you, unbiased stranger!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A secret society of Donald Trump look-alikes end up with all your money.

transcript.speaker: Trump look-alike
transcript.text: You're fired.

transcript.speaker: Trump look-alike
transcript.text: You are!

setting: Dogbert's desk, offices, a laboratory-style accountant's desk, and an investor's living room
situation: Dogbert lectures on how the stock market works, walking through the chain from employees giving data, to managers and the CEO spinning it, to accountants hiding bad news in footnotes. A home investor then takes advice from a TV pundit he thinks is unbiased. In the end, a group of Donald Trump look-alikes ends up with all the investors' money.
punchline: The stock market is a chain of spin, obfuscation and herd behavior from the factory floor to the TV, and the only winners are a cabal of rich insiders who take everyone's money.
summary: A cynical dog traces how corporate information gets massaged at every level until gullible investors hand their savings to a clique of tycoons.
keywords: didn't know I had a project

title: Boss Accidentally Insults Carol Over Copies

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My secretary is off, and I need to make copies of this...

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Oh, I get it! You immediately ask the only woman in the department to do it. #!%*☆$!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was going to ask where the copy machine is, but this works, too.

situation: The Boss mentions his secretary is off and that he needs copies made. Carol assumes he is expecting her, as the only woman in the department, to do the copying, and she angrily curses at him and shoves the paper back. The Boss reveals he only meant to ask where the copy machine was, but he is content to let her think otherwise.
punchline: The Boss realizes Carol's misunderstanding is more convenient than the truth, since it may get her to make the copies anyway, or at least he gets away with his laziness.
summary: A manager's innocent request is read as sexist by a coworker, and he quietly decides her mistaken outburst suits him just fine.

file: 2004/2004-03-16_over paid_4 dollars_honest_reports mistake_bowels of bureaucarzy_correct injustice.gif
title: Keep The Four Dollar Overpayment

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There is an error on my tiny paycheck. It is four dollars too much.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gasp!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now you must travel to the bowels of the bureaucracy to correct this injustice.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or I could just keep it as a reward for my honesty.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bowels I say!!!

situation: Dilbert honestly reports that his paycheck is four dollars too high. The Boss gasps and tells him he must now journey into the depths of the company bureaucracy to get it corrected. Dilbert suggests keeping the money as a reward for his honesty, and the Boss angrily insists on the bureaucratic route.
punchline: The company punishes honesty with a burdensome bureaucratic process and will not let an employee keep a trivial overpayment as a reward, showing how absurdly rigid and unrewarding the system is.
summary: An employee who flags a small payroll overpayment is sent off to wrestle with red tape rather than thanked for his integrity.

title: Tina Gets the Better Lunch Deal

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Tina, would you like to go to lunch with me?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: As a coworker or as a date?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: As a respected colleague.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Sounds fishy.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I know you're up to something; I just don't know what.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: You're getting the better deal. I'll be looking at your face but you get to look at me.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Maybe you could hike up your jacket to cover your face.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Fair enough.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: This is not a date. I insist on paying fifty percent.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I'll have the miser salad and water.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'll have three half-priced New York steaks.

situation: Ted invites Tina to lunch as a coworker, and she suspects an ulterior motive. He insists she is getting the better deal because she gets to look at him, and she insults his looks by suggesting he cover his face with his jacket. When she insists on splitting the bill, Ted orders a cheap salad while Tina orders three steaks.
punchline: By insisting on paying fifty percent, Tina turns the tables on Ted and orders a huge expensive meal, making him pay half for it as revenge for his vanity and ulterior motive.
summary: A coworker's smug lunch invitation backfires when his colleague uses a split-the-bill rule to order a feast at his expense.

file: 2004/2004-06-26_low pay_unpleasant work enviornment_applicants_miss old days_dental plan.gif
title: Dental Plan: Duck Or Get Hit

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't find any highly trained job applicants who want an unpleasant work environment and low pay.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I miss the old days where a man would build a skyscraper with his bare hands just to make you stop hitting him with a shovel.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did they have a dental plan?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Yes. They called it "Duck!!!"

situation: The Boss complains to Catbert, the HR director, that no skilled applicants want a miserable job with low pay. Catbert reminisces about a past era when workers would build skyscrapers barehanded to avoid being hit with a shovel. The Boss asks if they had a dental plan, and Catbert says their only plan was to duck.
punchline: Catbert reveals that the only 'dental plan' for abusive employers was dodging the blows, implying that the workplace has always been brutal and management longs for workers too desperate or intimidated to demand anything.
summary: A frustrated boss can't hire talent for a rotten job, and his HR cat fondly recalls the days when brutality alone kept workers in line.

file: 2004/2004-09-05_product development_two thirds_features_reduce scope_change request_stacks of paper_mean_unethical_passive agressive.gif
title: Free Change Requests Pile Up

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our budget won't cover all of the product development.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We can only do two-thirds of the features for that amount.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Reduce the scope of the project by one-third.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But... theoretically...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No... Dear Lord, no.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I later give you a change request to add one feature, could you do it for the same budget.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One? Sure.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Data goes in; management comes out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One? Sure.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Changes are free.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where do I put the change requests?

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle area and the Boss's office
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss the budget only covers two-thirds of the features, so the Boss has him cut the scope by a third. The Boss then asks, 'theoretically', whether a later change request for one feature could be done for the same budget, and Dilbert agrees to one. The Boss takes this to mean changes are free, and Dilbert ends up buried under a stack of change requests.
punchline: Dilbert's innocent agreement to absorb a single change request is twisted by the Boss into a blanket policy that all changes are free, leaving Dilbert drowning in paperwork.
summary: After trimming a project to fit its budget, a worker concedes one small extra request and watches it snowball into an unlimited pile of free changes.

title: Open Plan Mime Class

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Cubicles are too expensive. We're moving to an open plan.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You'll attend a special class to ease your transition.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's like he's in a cubicle with invisible walls!

setting: Catbert's office, then a training class
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells employees that cubicles are too expensive and the company is moving to an open plan. He sends them to a special class to ease the transition. In the class, a mime in a clown outfit pretends to feel invisible walls, and Dilbert observes that it looks like he is in a cubicle with invisible walls.
punchline: The company's cost-cutting open plan is absurdly taught through mime training, which simply recreates cubicle walls in imagination, so employees lose their cubicles but are asked to pretend the walls are still there.
summary: To save money HR scraps cubicles and sends staff to a mime-led class where they learn to act as though invisible walls still surround them.

file: 2004/2004-09-13_daughter sneezed_work from home_answer boss phone_phone messages aren't real_bitung humor.gif
title: Boss's Phone Messages Aren't Real

transcript.speaker: Boss's Assistant
transcript.text: My daughter sneezed so the school is sending her home.

transcript.speaker: Boss's Assistant
transcript.text: I'll work from home for the rest of the day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How will you answer my phone?

transcript.speaker: Boss's Assistant
transcript.text: I probably shouldn't tell you this, but none of your phone messages are real.

situation: The Boss's assistant tells him she needs to work from home because her daughter sneezed and the school is sending her home. The Boss asks how she will answer his phone. She admits that none of his phone messages are real, meaning no one actually calls him.
punchline: The assistant reveals that the boss's phone never really rings with genuine messages, so her absence won't matter at all, which exposes how irrelevant he is.
summary: An assistant heading home to care for her child casually confesses that the phone messages she has been giving her boss were never genuine.

title: Mumbling As Work-Avoidance Strategy

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've added mumbling and peevishness to my work-avoidance arsenal.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I get the benefits of appearing knowledgeable without the burden of sharing.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Um... I didn't hear what you said.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sheeesh!!!

situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug beside Dilbert at the coffee maker, explains that he has added mumbling and peevishness to his repertoire of ways to avoid work. He says it makes him seem knowledgeable without having to share anything. Alice then walks up and says she couldn't hear him, and Wally responds with an exasperated 'Sheeesh!'
punchline: Wally demonstrates his new technique immediately by getting huffy when Alice asks him to repeat himself, proving that mumbling and peevishness successfully shield him from having to share anything.
summary: A lazy employee boasts that muttering and acting irritated lets him look smart while contributing nothing, then promptly shows it off when a colleague asks him to repeat himself.

title: Misguided Optimism of Online Resume Submission

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Click "submit" to post your resume on the jobs web site.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now sit back and enjoy the misguided optimism that someday a human being will see it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Be sure to tell your parents that you looked for a job today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Niece
transcript.text: I'll e-mail them.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dilbert sits on the couch helping a young woman with a laptop post her resume on an online jobs web site. He wryly tells her to enjoy the hope that a human will ever read it, then reminds her to tell her parents she looked for work. She calmly replies that she will e-mail them.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcasm implies that online resume submissions vanish into a void, so the only real result of the job search is being able to claim you made an effort.
summary: While helping a young woman upload her resume online, Dilbert cynically suggests the effort is mostly useful for reassuring her family.

title: Best Employer Without Spending Anything

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our corporate goal is to become one of Fortune magazine's top 100 companies to work for!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We hope to do it without giving you any additional money, benefits or freedom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then how could you possibly motivate us to say we're happy to work...uh-oh.

situation: The Boss announces to his employees at a meeting table that the company wants to be named one of Fortune's best places to work. He adds that he won't provide any extra pay, benefits or freedom to achieve it. Dilbert wonders how the staff could then be motivated to claim they're happy, and a hooded figure with a whip appears behind them.
punchline: Since management won't improve actual working conditions, the only way to get employees to say they're happy is through threats and coercion.
summary: A manager wants a best-employer ranking for free, and the only motivational tool left is a whip-wielding enforcer standing behind the staff.

title: Therapist Insults Dilbert's Looks

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have uncontrollable urges to show people better ways to do things.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you think the real issue might be my insecurity?

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: Well, I wouldn't date you, but that's mostly because of your looks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not helping.

situation: Dilbert lies on a couch and tells his therapist he has an uncontrollable urge to show people better ways to do things. He wonders aloud whether his insecurity is the real problem. The therapist responds by saying she wouldn't date him because of his looks.
punchline: Dilbert asks for reassurance about his insecurity and the therapist instead delivers a blunt insult about his appearance, making her about the least helpful therapist possible.
summary: A patient seeking insight into his insecurity gets an unexpectedly tactless remark about his appearance from his counselor.

file: 2004/2004-12-12_cubicle vampire_happy coowrkers_in search of_talk_work related issues_life drained_gut instinct_you're hire.gif
title: The Cubicle Vampire Gets Hired

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Job interview

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's your biggest weakness.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I'm a cubicle vampire.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I wander the cubicles in search of happy coworkers.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Then I pounce!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then you suck their blood?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: That was the old way.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I talk about work-related issues until the life is drained from their bodies.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm going to trust my gut instinct on this.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're hired.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you met the new hire yet?

setting: A job interview room, then an office cubicle
situation: The Boss interviews a candidate and asks about her biggest weakness. She describes herself as a cubicle vampire who seeks out happy coworkers and drains the life from them by talking endlessly about work-related issues. The Boss hires her on the spot, and in the last panel Dilbert is slumped at his desk, drained and lifeless.
punchline: The Boss treats a candidate who destroys employee morale as a great hire, and the drained Dilbert shows the cost of that decision.
summary: A job applicant cheerfully confesses to killing her colleagues' spirits with endless shop talk, and the oblivious manager hires her anyway.

title: Happy Place Is a Coffee Toilet

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll escape the horror of this meeting by taking my mind to a happy place.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Aaah... a pool of warm coffee; what could be better?

setting: Conference room during a meeting, then Wally's imagined fantasy
situation: The Boss talks at the conference table while Wally, sitting next to Dilbert, mentally checks out and imagines a happy place. His fantasy is soaking in a giant mug of warm coffee. In the last panel the fantasy reveals itself as a toilet-like setup with a donut on a chain and a tank above, with Wally reading the news.
punchline: Wally's idea of a happy place is a giant coffee-mug bathtub that doubles as a toilet, perfectly combining his love of coffee, donuts and avoiding work.
summary: Bored in a meeting, Wally daydreams about lounging in a giant cup of coffee that turns out to be a cozy restroom retreat.

file: 2004/2004-05-23_performance review_meetings_too negative_poo posed ideas_cold fusion_perpetual motion_clothes dryer_antigravity pants_mri vending machine_terrible ideas_negative attitude_tongue scraper.gif
title: Punished for Calling Ideas Terrible

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Performance review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: People say you're too negative in meetings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Negative? When?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: According to the marketing department. You poo-pooed a number of their ideas...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...the cold fusion scooter, perpetual motion clothes dryer, antigravity pants, MRI vending machine, and the list goes on.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Those are terrible ideas!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Negative attitude!!! Gottcha!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, you're right. From now on, I will support all terrible ideas.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Employee
transcript.text: It's a tongue scraper and a frozen flagpole!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can it be electrified?

setting: Boss's office during a performance review, then a meeting room
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert in a performance review that marketing complains he is too negative about their ideas. When Dilbert points out the ideas, such as an antigravity pants and an MRI vending machine, are terrible, the Boss pounces on his negativity. Dilbert vows to support every terrible idea and, in the next meeting, eagerly encourages a ridiculous tongue scraper and frozen flagpole product.
punchline: Dilbert is punished for honestly criticizing absurd ideas, so he malicious-compliantly cheers on a ridiculous product and even suggests making it more dangerous by electrifying it.
summary: After being reprimanded for dismissing marketing's absurd inventions, an employee swears to back every awful idea and gleefully makes the next one worse.

title: Business Case For Doing Nothing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We only have two people on the third floor. Let's move them to our empty cubes here and sublet the space.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Write a business case with all the risks and business drivers and I'll consider it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I changed my mind. We shouldn't do anything.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need a business case for that, too.

situation: Dilbert proposes consolidating two employees from the third floor into empty cubes and subletting the freed-up space. The Boss demands a full business case covering risks and business drivers before he will consider it. Dilbert tries to escape the paperwork by withdrawing the idea, but the Boss insists on a business case for doing nothing as well.
punchline: Bureaucratic demands for justification are so rigid that even deciding to take no action requires a formal business case, so there is no way to avoid the paperwork.
summary: A simple cost-saving suggestion gets buried in red tape, and even abandoning it turns out to need official documentation.

file: 2004/2004-03-23_speak at school_sons school_disguise bitterness_punish son_honored to speak.gif
title: Career Day As Parental Punishment

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Would you consider speaking at my son's school on "Career Day"?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'd do it myself but I can't disguise the bitterness and despair that gnaw at my soul.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Plus my son has been bad and I told him I'd punish him.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd be honored to speak.

situation: Carol, the Boss's assistant, asks him to speak at her son's school on Career Day. She explains that she can't do it herself because she couldn't hide her bitterness and despair about her job, and adds that her son has been bad and she promised to punish him. The Boss, missing the insult, happily says he'd be honored to speak.
punchline: Carol is sending the Boss to Career Day as a punishment for her son, implying the Boss is dreadful to listen to, and he obliviously takes it as a compliment.
summary: A weary assistant volunteers her clueless boss as a Career Day speaker precisely because listening to him will serve as discipline for her misbehaving child.

title: Too Dumb to Read Email

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I called this meeting so I could tell you the division's goals for next year.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's a good idea because we're all so dumb that we couldn't possibly read this in e-mail.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Goal one: Improve communication.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can't; I'm too dumb.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: A manager holding a sheet of paper calls a meeting just to announce the division's goals. Alice sarcastically says the staff are too dumb to read the goals in an e-mail. When the manager announces the first goal, improving communication, Alice throws her dumbness line back at him, refusing to take it on.
punchline: Alice's sarcasm turns the manager's implied insult back on him: if everyone is too dumb to read an e-mail, they are too dumb to improve communication, and the meeting itself shows the manager's communication is the problem.
summary: A manager convenes a meeting to read out goals that could have been emailed, and a sarcastic employee uses his own low opinion of the staff to dodge the first goal.

title: Recognition Meeting Costs More Than Savings

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Kudos to Ted for his suggestion to put motion sensors on the lights in the break room.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hold it! I calculate that the energy savings are offset by the lost productivity of this meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We have to burn the plaque for heat just to break even.

situation: The Boss publicly praises Ted for suggesting motion sensors on the break room lights, presumably to present him with an award. Dilbert interrupts to point out that the time wasted in the recognition meeting costs more than the energy saved. He concludes they would have to burn the commemorative plaque for heat just to break even.
punchline: The ceremony honoring an energy-saving idea wastes so much employee time that it wipes out the savings, making the recognition itself a net loss.
summary: An award ceremony for a power-saving suggestion turns out to cost more in lost work time than the idea could ever save.

file: 2004/2004-08-27_evil director_himan resources_cheaper_employee wellness program_sick days_incentives_highly paid workers_more fun.gif
title: Cheaper: Wellness Program Or Death

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I can't decide what's cheaper...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: ...an employee wellness program to reduce sick days or incentivizing the older, highly paid workers to die.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you could use math to figure it out.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: When I said cheaper, I meant more fun.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells The Boss he can't decide which is cheaper: a wellness program to cut sick days or encouraging older, highly paid employees to die. The Boss suggests he simply calculate the costs with math. Catbert reveals that cost was never his real criterion.
punchline: Catbert's real decision criterion isn't cost at all but which option is more entertaining to him, exposing HR cost-cutting talk as a cover for cruelty.
summary: A malicious HR chief weighs health perks against pushing expensive veterans toward an early grave, then admits he's only choosing whichever is more amusing.

title: Rewarding Top Performers With Workload

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Job applicant

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant
transcript.text: How do you reward your top performers?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I keep increasing their workloads until their performances become average.

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant
transcript.text: So...why would anyone try to excel?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I use only the finest motivational posters.

situation: A job applicant asks the Pointy-Haired Boss how he rewards his best employees. The Boss admits he piles on more work until high performers sink to average. When the applicant asks why anyone would try to excel, the Boss says he relies on motivational posters.
punchline: The Boss punishes excellence with extra work and then offers only cheap motivational posters as encouragement, showing management that destroys the very motivation it claims to inspire.
summary: A manager cheerfully confesses that his reward for great work is so much extra work that stars become mediocre, with decorative posters as his only incentive.

title: Collateral for Borrowing a Chair

transcript.speaker: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.text: May I borrow your chair for a meeting?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, but leave your wallet, keys, company I.D. and one shoe with me.

transcript.speaker: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.text: I'm your Chief Financial Officer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then I also need your PDA and one sock.

situation: A man asks Dilbert if he can borrow his chair for a meeting. Dilbert agrees only if the man leaves his wallet, keys, company ID and a shoe as collateral. When the man points out he is the company's Chief Financial Officer, Dilbert responds by demanding even more items.
punchline: Dilbert treats a senior executive's request like a pawn-shop loan, and the man's high rank only makes Dilbert raise the collateral instead of relenting.
summary: Dilbert demands a pile of personal belongings as a deposit before lending his office chair, and refuses to ease up even when the borrower turns out to be a top executive.

title: Spam Pills Meet Ginkgo Biloba

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm addicted to spam. I can't resist it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Last week I bought every pill that was offered and took them at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let me tell you, there are a few pills you don't want to mix with the ginkgo biloba.

situation: Wally sits at a meeting table with Dilbert and The Boss and confesses that he is addicted to spam email. He explains that he bought and swallowed every pill advertised to him all at once. He then warns that some of those pills react badly with ginkgo biloba.
