punchline: Wally blindly trusts spam advertisements and swallows every pill at once, then casually offers drug-interaction advice as if mass self-medication from junk email were a normal hobby.
summary: A cheerful coworker admits he gulped down every pill he was spammed about and now dispenses advice on dangerous combinations.

file: 2004/2004-03-11_repeat customer_rate of recidivism_focus on marketing_learn from experience_free knuckle tattoo_nicknames for women_free book_criminals_dumb.gif
title: Marketing to Repeat Offenders

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We only have a 10% repeat customer rate whereas prisons have a 70% rate of recidivism.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to focus our marketing on criminals because they don't learn from experience.

transcript.speaker: Television Ad
transcript.text: Order now and get a free knuckle tattoo plus our free book "1,001 nicknames for women."

setting: Conference room, then a living room with a TV
situation: In a meeting, the Boss compares the company's poor 10% repeat customer rate to the 70% recidivism rate of prisons and concludes the company should market to criminals. The final panel shows a tough-looking bald, bearded man in a recliner watching an ad that offers a free knuckle tattoo and a book of nicknames for women.
punchline: The Boss reasons that criminals are ideal repeat customers because they never learn from experience, and the resulting ad is hilariously tailored to a stereotypical thug.
summary: A manager decides to chase the customer loyalty of ex-cons, and the resulting infomercial targets a tattooed tough guy on his couch.

title: Boss Bluffs EBITDA Definition

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, Dilbert, what are you doing for the EBITDA today?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The what?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: EBITDA means the earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and um...ammonia.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you sure about ammonia?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why must you be so accretive?

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert what he is doing for the EBITDA today, then, when Dilbert doesn't know the term, tries to explain it. He gets the last word of the acronym wrong, substituting 'ammonia' for 'amortization.' When Dilbert questions it, the Boss deflects by accusing him of being 'accretive.'
punchline: The Boss uses a financial acronym he doesn't actually understand, invents a nonsense word to fill the gap, and then dodges correction by misusing another piece of finance jargon ('accretive') as an insult.
summary: A manager confidently tosses around a finance buzzword, flubs its definition with a silly chemical, and answers a fair challenge with more misapplied jargon.

title: Huge Obstacle Means Mild Inconvenience

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: My progress has been thwarted by a huge obstacle.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I.e. everything I need to do is inconvenient.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: You can take my soul but not my lack of enthusiasm.

situation: At a meeting table, a bald, bespectacled coworker gives a status update to the Boss and Dilbert. He claims a huge obstacle has thwarted his progress, then admits the obstacle is simply that all his tasks are inconvenient. He ends by proudly declaring his lack of enthusiasm unbreakable.
punchline: The employee dramatically blames a 'huge obstacle' for his lack of progress, but it turns out he just doesn't want to do inconvenient work, and he defiantly clings to his apathy as his last bit of dignity.
summary: A disengaged employee dresses up plain laziness as a major roadblock during a status meeting and then boasts that his apathy is the one thing management can't take from him.

title: Attitude Problem Meets Terrifying Smile

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why does the new engineer get paid more than I do? How do you justify that??!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Unlike you, he doesn't have a bad attitude.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I have a good attitude! Look at this smile! Look!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My eyes!!!

situation: Alice storms into the Boss's office and demands to know why a newly hired engineer earns more than she does. The Boss coolly blames her bad attitude. She responds by flashing an aggressive, toothy grin to prove her attitude is good, and the Boss recoils in horror.
punchline: Alice's furious, forced smile proves her bad attitude better than anything, and the Boss's pained reaction confirms it.
summary: An underpaid employee tries to prove her sunny disposition with a menacing grimace that horrifies her manager.

title: Bottleneck Bill's Delay Philosophy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bottleneck Bill

transcript.speaker: Bottleneck Bill
transcript.text: Perhaps you're wondering why I haven't answered your e-mails.

transcript.speaker: Bottleneck Bill
transcript.text: My philosophy is that anything worth doing is worth delaying.

transcript.speaker: Bottleneck Bill
transcript.text: Plus you look like that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Like what?

situation: Dilbert visits a coworker named Bottleneck Bill, who is sitting at his desk. Bill explains that he has ignored Dilbert's e-mails because he believes anything worth doing is worth delaying. He then adds a personal insult, saying Dilbert looks like that, and Dilbert asks what he means.
punchline: Bill's lazy excuse for procrastinating is topped by an unexplained insult, which suggests he simply doesn't like Dilbert and is dodging work out of spite.
summary: A chronically slow coworker justifies ignoring requests with a procrastination creed, then tacks on a vague jab at the visitor's appearance.

title: Boss Busy With Miscellaneous Things

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need your help forcing Bottleneck Bill to do his job so I can do my job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll be all over that...as soon as I finish other things.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What other things?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, for example, miscellaneous.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss to step in and make a colleague named Bottleneck Bill do his work, because Bill is holding up Dilbert's own job. The boss says he will deal with it after he finishes other things. When Dilbert asks what those things are, the boss gives a vague non-answer.
punchline: The boss's excuse for not helping is a vague catch-all category, 'miscellaneous', which shows he has no real tasks and is simply avoiding doing his job.
summary: A manager brushes off a request to deal with a bottleneck coworker by claiming to be busy with unspecified odds and ends.

title: Elbonian Call Center's Exaggerated American Accents

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Elbonian call center

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: Remember to use your American accents!

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Agent
transcript.text: Yee-haa!! Let's put the dawg in the Chevy! Look at the size of my missiles!!

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: We only do it that way in the cafeteria.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Agent
transcript.text: Oops. Sorry.

setting: An Elbonian call center with rows of workers at computers wearing headsets
situation: A supervisor with a megaphone reminds the Elbonian call center staff to use American accents on calls. One agent responds by shouting a string of exaggerated, nonsensical American-sounding phrases. The supervisor points out that this is only how they talk in the cafeteria, and the agent apologizes.
punchline: The Elbonians' idea of an American accent is a ridiculous caricature of redneck slang and bravado, and they apparently practice it as a casual game over lunch.
summary: Offshore phone workers rehearse a cartoonish version of American speech, and their boss merely objects to where they are doing it.

title: Dogbert Explains the Nose Fairy

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Why does a runny nose stop running when you fall asleep?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The Nose Fairy sneaks in at night and pinches your nostrils shut.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is exactly why I don't like knowledge.

setting: Dogbert's living room, then Dilbert's bedroom at night
situation: Ratbert asks Dogbert why a runny nose stops running during sleep. Dogbert gives a made-up, creepy answer about a Nose Fairy who sneaks in and pinches your nostrils shut. In the final panel Dilbert lies in bed with Ratbert beside him, thinking about how he dislikes knowledge.
punchline: Dogbert's invented explanation is so unsettling that the now-informed Dilbert can't sleep peacefully, which makes him wish he'd never learned it.
summary: A dog's absurd bedtime explanation for why noses stop dripping leaves a listener lying awake and wishing he were less informed.

title: Technically Our Customers Kill Themselves

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our revenue is now double the number of people that our product has killed... recently.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Our product costs $80. Are you saying that each one kills 40 people?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our customers know the health risks, so technically they're killing themselves.

transcript.speaker: Unknown speaker
transcript.text: So technically we aren't scum?

situation: The Boss presents a chart comparing the company's revenue to the number of people its product has killed, proudly noting revenue is double. An employee points out the absurd math implied by the $80 price, and the Boss shifts blame to customers who knew the risks. A coworker then asks whether that means the company isn't scum.
punchline: The Boss uses a hairsplitting technicality to dodge moral responsibility for a deadly product, and the sarcastic question exposes that the company is still obviously scum.
summary: A manager brags about profits outpacing the body count of a lethal product, then argues the customers are really to blame.

file: 2004/2004-08-22_girlfriend_two probelms_looks_personlaity_extreme makeover_fascinated by new person_9 good tsories_social liability_relationships.gif
title: Dilbert's Nine Good Stories Limit

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why can't I find a girlfriend?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You have two problems: your looks and your personality.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hmm...two isn't bad.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can fix my looks by getting an extreme makeover.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You'll still need to improve your M.T.T.S.F.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Mean time to story failure: it's a measure of how long you can be fascinating to a new person.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've been counting, and you only have nine good stories. After you use them up, you're a social liability.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I saw a horse kick a woodchuck over a fence.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Still only nine.

setting: Outdoors on a sidewalk and then a grassy hillside
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert why he can't find a girlfriend, and Dogbert tells him he has two problems: his looks and his personality. Dilbert optimistically proposes a makeover, but Dogbert introduces a made-up metric, mean time to story failure, and says Dilbert has only nine good stories. Dilbert tries to add a new anecdote, and Dogbert dismisses it.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to tell a tenth good story, about a horse kicking a woodchuck over a fence, fails to impress, confirming that his supply of interesting stories is stuck at nine.
summary: Dogbert coldly analyzes his friend's dating troubles with a mock-technical metric and rejects the one new story offered as proof of improvement.

file: 2004/2004-07-18_berating_humilation_importance of work_making sound rate products_motivate staff_no prasie_no raises_threats belittling_trophy wives.gif
title: Catbert Advises Boss on Motivation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need help motivating the staff.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: What have you already tried?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Threats, belittling, humiliation, empty promises, berating, slogans, posters and bullying.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Hmm...We can't praise them or else they'd ask for raises.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Maybe they can be motivated by the importance of their work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Their work is making second-rate products to sell to idiots so our executives can afford trophy wives.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Have you tried yelling until your face turns purple?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make three copies, please!!!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: This is new.

setting: Catbert's office and a nearby office area
situation: The Boss asks Catbert, the evil HR director, for help motivating the staff and lists all the cruel tactics he has already used. Catbert suggests avoiding praise so nobody asks for raises, then floats appealing to the importance of their work, which the Boss admits is making shoddy products for executives' trophy wives. Catbert suggests yelling until his face turns purple, and in the last panel the Boss, purple-faced, screams a photocopy request at a bewildered employee.
punchline: The Boss's idea of a new management technique is simply shouting a trivial request until he turns purple, and the employee notes it's something new only because he's never been this ridiculous about copies.
summary: After exhausting every kind of bullying, a boss gets one more cruel tip from HR and tries it out on a clerk making copies.

title: Boss Mangles Instructions Over Bad Connection

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have a bad connection, so listen carefully.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Throw... my... desk... off... building...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope that sounded like "Go through my desk and office and find the billing codes."

setting: The Boss's car and Dilbert's office
situation: The Boss calls Dilbert from his car on a cell phone and warns that the connection is bad, so Dilbert must listen carefully. The garbled message Dilbert hears is an instruction to throw the Boss's desk off the building, and Dilbert agrees to do it. The Boss then hopes his message came through as a request to find the billing codes.
punchline: The Boss's warning about listening carefully is useless because the broken-up call turns a simple request into a destructive order, and he only realizes the risk after Dilbert has already said okay.
summary: A manager phoning from his car in a dead zone gives instructions that reach his employee as a command to destroy the office furniture.

title: Alice Admits Ignoring Clueless Assignments

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I've been told that you ignore your team's assignments and work on things that aren't your job.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's true. I do important things instead of useless things assigned by clueless nimrods.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You totally ruined this meeting.

situation: The Boss sits across a desk from Alice and confronts her with a report that she skips her team's assignments to work on things outside her job. Alice cheerfully admits it and explains she does important work instead of useless tasks handed out by clueless people. The Boss, rather than reprimanding her, complains that she has ruined his meeting.
punchline: Alice's blunt honesty denies the Boss the chance to scold her, and he is more upset about his meeting going off-script than about her insubordination or the insult to management.
summary: Confronted about dodging assigned work, Alice cheerfully owns up and insults the people handing out the tasks, leaving her boss annoyed that his meeting has been spoiled.

file: 2004/2004-12-22_objectives are vague_unmeasurable_not inspired_achieve full ptential_bad job.gif
title: Complaining About Vague Objectives Backfires

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I am concerned because my objectives are vague and unmeasurable.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As a result, I am not inspired to achieve my full potential...and... um...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did I just say I'm doing a bad job and ask you to punish me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's what I heard.

situation: Dilbert stands in front of the Boss's desk and voices a concern that his work objectives are vague and unmeasurable, saying he feels uninspired. Mid-sentence he realizes how his complaint might sound and asks whether he just admitted to doing a bad job and requested punishment. The Boss confirms that is exactly how he interpreted it.
punchline: The Boss twists Dilbert's constructive feedback about unclear goals into a self-admission of poor performance, showing that managers hear criticism as a confession.
summary: An employee raising a fair complaint about unclear goals discovers his boss has understood it as a plea for punishment.

title: The Buck-Passer's Tear-Away Shirt

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Buck-Passer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have a do-it for you...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The one day that I don't wear my tear-away shirt, and this happens!

situation: The Boss approaches a group of employees holding a piece of paper, announcing that he has a 'do-it' for someone. When he hands it over, one employee is grabbed by a coworker and flung into the Boss's path, and ends up holding the paper. The victim complains that this had to happen on the one day he isn't wearing his tear-away shirt.
punchline: The employee has so routinely been grabbed and shoved forward to take the blame or work that he normally wears a tear-away shirt to escape, implying this is a regular office ritual.
summary: A manager hands out an unwanted task, and the staff cheerfully sacrifice a colleague who lacks his usual escape clothing.

title: Only One Sober Person Here

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I see a problem with your plan.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oh, do you, Mr. Negativity?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why is it that you're the o-o-o-only person in this meeting to see a problem? Huh? Huh?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My theory is that the rest of you are either morons or drunk.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I am totally sober!

situation: Dilbert points out a flaw in a coworker's plan during a meeting. The coworker sarcastically calls him negative and demands to know why he alone sees a problem. Dilbert calmly replies that everyone else must be morons or drunk, and the coworker defensively insists he is sober.
punchline: Dilbert insults the whole room by implying the lack of objections means everyone is either stupid or drunk, and the coworker only bothers to deny being drunk, tacitly accepting the moron label.
summary: A man mocks Dilbert for being the lone critic of his plan, and Dilbert's explanation for the silence of everyone else leaves him protesting only one of the two insults.

file: 2004/2004-09-26_blindfold_carbs_cublicle_heinous crime_put new guy_won't know blind fold_finance troll.gif
title: Hell Is Out of Space, Try Cubicles

transcript.speaker: Caption
transcript.text: Heck

transcript.speaker: Green Demon
transcript.text: We're out of space, boss.

transcript.speaker: Green Demon
transcript.text: We've had a big upswing in people who use cell phones in bathrooms.

transcript.speaker: Red Devil
transcript.text: Dang. I've got a new guy coming in today. Where will I put him?

transcript.speaker: Green Demon
transcript.text: Maybe you could ask your brother.

transcript.speaker: Red Devil
transcript.text: Hmm...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, I suppose you could put him in a cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Red Devil
transcript.text: His crime wasn't that heinous.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, if you blindfold him, he won't know he's in a cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Blindfolded Man
transcript.text: So then I find out that it's not okay to eat carbs.

setting: Hell (with a final panel in an office cubicle area)
situation: A green demon tells the red devil in charge of Hell that they have run out of room because of an influx of people who use cell phones in bathrooms. The devil asks his brother, the Boss, where to put the new arrival, and the Boss suggests a cubicle. The devil says that's too harsh a punishment, so the Boss suggests blindfolding the new arrival so he won't realize where he is, and in the last panel a blindfolded man is standing in a cubicle.
punchline: Cubicles are considered a punishment so cruel that even Hell's devil thinks they are too harsh for a minor offender, and the Boss's idea of blindfolding someone to hide it only works until he finds out in other ways.
summary: When Hell fills up with bathroom cell phone users, the devil's brother recommends the cruel fate of an office cubicle, which the devil thinks is too severe unless the victim is kept blindfolded.

title: Removing Body Parts for Time Off

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where were you last week?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I had my coccyx removed.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm having all of my unnecessary body parts removed so I can get time off from work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about the part of your brain that makes you care about others?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's on my list after tonsils.

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker
situation: Dilbert asks a bald, bespectacled coworker where he was last week, and the coworker says he had his coccyx removed. He explains he is having all his unnecessary body parts surgically removed to get time off work. Dilbert suggests he remove the part of his brain responsible for caring about others, and the coworker says it is already on his list.
punchline: The coworker is so selfish and so desperate to avoid work that he treats the part of the brain that gives him empathy as just another removable organ, to be scheduled after his tonsils.
summary: A coworker proudly admits he is surgically shedding spare organs in order to rack up sick days, and cheerfully agrees that his capacity for empathy is next.

title: Wally Avoids Communication With Earwax

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My voice mailbox is full, and my spam filter rejects all incoming e-mail.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: As soon as I build up a good load of ear wax, I'll be off the grid.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, we need to talk.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Eh?

situation: Wally sits at a meeting table with his coffee and explains that he has made himself unreachable by voicemail and email. He says that once he builds up enough ear wax he will be completely off the grid. The Boss then says they need to talk, and Wally pretends he can't hear him.
punchline: Wally's final barrier against being contacted is his own ear wax, and he demonstrates it instantly by feigning deafness when the boss tries to speak to him.
summary: A lazy employee brags about layering up defenses against every way of being contacted, then fakes hearing loss the moment his manager approaches.

file: 2004/2004-03-26_rat_meeting_walls spot_seat filler_proedcest day_career work out_look at me now_fired_business.gif
title: Dogbert Seat-Fills for Wally

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wally is in the men's room. I've accepted a position as his seat filler.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is the proudest day of my life. I never imagined that my career would work out so well.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I want to scream to the world, "Look at me now!"

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: False alarm. You're fired.

situation: Dogbert sits in Wally's chair at a meeting table, explaining that he has taken a job as Wally's seat filler while Wally is in the men's room. He gushes about how proud he is of his career success and wants to shout it to the world. Wally then returns and dismisses him from the job.
punchline: Dogbert's career peak, filling an empty seat for someone using the restroom, lasts only moments before he is fired, mocking both the triviality of the job and his overblown pride.
summary: A dog celebrates the pinnacle of his career as a stand-in for an absent coworker, only to lose the gig the moment the coworker returns.

file: 2004/2004-05-15_workplace injuries_10 thousand percent_new safety manuals_website_blood pressure rising_technology.gif
title: Cursed Safety Manual Binders Injure Staff

transcript.speaker: Human Resources Director
transcript.text: Workplace injuries are up ten thousand percent since I distributed the new safety manuals.

transcript.speaker: Human Resources Director
transcript.text: The binders have sharp edges and, apparently, a curse. I asked Asok to help put it on our web site.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Hands...so numb. Eyes...strained. Blood pressure rising...

situation: The HR director tells the bandaged Boss and Dilbert that workplace injuries have skyrocketed since he handed out the new safety manuals. The binders have sharp edges and seem cursed, so he had Asok put the manual on the company web site. Asok is then shown at his computer, numb-handed, eye-strained and with rising blood pressure, apparently injured by the task.
punchline: The safety manual meant to prevent injuries is itself so hazardous that it injures everyone who touches it, even in its digital form, which makes the whole safety program counterproductive.
summary: A safety initiative backfires when the manual that was supposed to protect employees ends up hurting everyone who handles it, including the intern assigned to digitize it.

title: Wally's Stress-Free Petty Theft

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, how can you be so stress-free?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's quite simple.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Stress is caused by an unrealistic belief that people care about you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I, on the other hand, expect people to be like me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let's visit Ted and I'll show you how this works.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ted, do you have the budget numbers that you promised me?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: That's next on my to-do list.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: While he was lying to me, I stole his stapler, so I came out ahead.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: He forgot his mug. I'm going to slip that puppy into my briefcase.

situation: Dilbert asks Wally why he is so stress-free, and Wally explains that stress comes from believing people care about you. He demonstrates by asking Ted for promised budget numbers; Ted brushes him off with a lie while Wally steals Ted's stapler. In the last panel Ted notices Wally left his mug behind and plans to steal it.
punchline: Wally's philosophy of expecting everyone to be as selfish and dishonest as he is works perfectly, since Ted immediately proves it by planning to steal Wally's mug.
summary: Wally explains his calm outlook on coworkers by assuming everyone is as dishonest as he is, then trades a stolen stapler for a mug about to be pilfered.

file: 2004/2004-08-19_product design_consumer electronics_form emotional bond_ego influenced_design process.gif
title: Egg-Shaped Product With Wagging Tail

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Product designer

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I bring you the future of product design for consumer electronics.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Behold nature's perfect shape! Your customers will form an emotional bond.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you think your ego influenced the design process?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bah!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's wagging.

setting: Conference room during a product design presentation
situation: Dogbert, posing as a product designer, stands on a stool and unveils a new consumer electronics device under a yellow cloth. The device is a smooth egg shape, which he claims is nature's perfect form that customers will bond with. When Dilbert asks if Dogbert's ego shaped the design, the Boss notices that the egg-shaped device has a little tail that is wagging.
punchline: The 'perfect shape' for consumer electronics turns out to be a self-portrait of Dogbert, complete with a wagging tail, confirming that his ego drove the design.
summary: A pompous product designer reveals his groundbreaking gadget, which suspiciously resembles a white egg version of himself.

file: 2004/2004-07-13_negotiate sale_voice activated hassock business_no lying_plenty of ommissions_tactical ignorance.gif
title: Boss Coaches Dishonest Negotiation Tactics

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to negotiate the sale of our voice activated hassock business.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're not allowed to lie, but I expect plenty of omissions, misdirections, exaggerations...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...unjustified optimism, lost documents, unclear explanations, gray areas and tactical ignorance. Oh, and say that we have other offers.

situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert to negotiate the sale of the company's voice activated hassock business. He says Dilbert may not lie, then lists a long series of deceptive tactics he expects, ending with an instruction to claim there are other offers, which is itself a lie.
punchline: The Boss forbids lying but then describes every dishonest technique short of it, and finishes by telling Dilbert to lie about having other offers, showing his ethics are purely cosmetic.
summary: A manager sends an employee to sell a doomed product line and insists on honesty while prescribing a catalogue of deceit.

file: 2004/2004-05-03_80 hour week_crazy talk_less work_loofah_evil director_human resources_business.gif
title: Catbert Recommends Tongue Bathing Instead

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm working 80 hours a week. I barely have time to bathe.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Try using your tongue during meetings. It's like a bath and a loofah all in one.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Or I could do less work.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That's crazy talk.

situation: A disheveled, overworked employee tells Catbert, the HR director, that her 80-hour work weeks leave her no time to bathe. Catbert suggests she lick herself during meetings as a combined bath and loofah. When she proposes simply working less, Catbert dismisses the idea as crazy.
punchline: HR's solution to employee overwork is to adapt to grooming like a cat rather than reduce the workload, since working less is unthinkable.
summary: An exhausted worker complains she has no time to wash, and the feline HR chief offers a cat-style cleaning hack instead of relief from her hours.

file: 2004/2004-03-14_day off_gerbil_heartless_horrible person_insensitive_mean_sisters weight_toss in casket_twin sister death.gif
title: Boss Mocks Twin Sister's Funeral Request

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I need a day off to attend my twin sister's funeral.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A whole day?? How well did you know her?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: She... was... my... twin.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But not identical!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How does that matter?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well... she didn't even look like you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And yet you want a whole day off for a service that takes fifteen minutes.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! It would be impossible to be more insensitive!!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll compromise. My pet gerbil is on his last legs. I'll give you the day off if you toss him in the casket so I don't have to bury him myself.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: When do you think it will die?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Depends. How much does your sister weigh?

situation: Alice asks her boss for a day off to attend her twin sister's funeral. He interrogates how well she knew her sister, argues that a non-identical twin barely counts, and complains that a fifteen-minute service doesn't need a whole day. When Alice explodes at his insensitivity, he offers a 'compromise': a day off if she buries his dying pet gerbil in the casket.
punchline: Alice, driven past outrage, ends up bargaining over the boss's callous deal and asks when the gerbil will die, only for him to ask how much her dead sister weighs, topping his own insensitivity.
summary: A manager grudgingly weighs a grieving employee's bereavement leave and then proposes she sneak his dying rodent into her sister's coffin.

title: Profits Given to Executives as Options

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll tell the stockholders that we earned $100 million!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will you tell them that you gave all of their profits to senior management in the form of unexpensed stock options?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We had to be incentivized.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So you wouldn't take their furniture, too?

situation: During a meeting, the boss announces he will tell the stockholders the company earned $100 million. Dilbert asks whether he will also admit that all of those profits went to senior management as unexpensed stock options. The boss justifies it by saying management needed incentives, and Dilbert sarcastically asks if that means they stopped short of taking the shareholders' furniture.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic question implies executives have taken everything of value from shareholders short of their furniture, and 'incentivized' is a flimsy excuse for self-dealing.
summary: A boss plans to brag about huge profits to investors while omitting that executives pocketed them all through stock options, and an employee mocks the justification.

file: 2004/2004-06-24_resume_stole stuff_great stuff_caught in parking lot_technically not stealing_buried german tourust_guilty_crazy_admits to bizarreness.gif
title: Job Candidate's Alarming Resume Confession

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: According to your resumé, you left your last job because you "allegedly stole lots of great stuff."

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Technically, if they catch you in the parking lot, and you give it back, that's not stealin'.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you buried a German tourist in your cellar.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: One time!

situation: The Boss interviews a job candidate and reads aloud from his resume, which says he left his last job over allegedly stealing. The candidate defends himself on a technicality about being caught in the parking lot. The Boss then raises that he buried a German tourist in his cellar, and the candidate protests that it only happened once.
punchline: The candidate treats burying a tourist in his cellar as a minor, forgivable lapse because it only happened one time, while the interviewer shows no alarm.
summary: A hiring interview turns grim when a applicant shrugs off a theft record and then half-admits to a murder in his basement.

title: Overpriced Servers Buy Dilbert's Departure

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I decided to buy all of our server upgrades through Bribertek, Inc.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: Are we buying overpriced hardware because they offered you a job?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because if we're paying extra to get rid of you, it's money well spent.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a coincidence!

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that all server upgrades will be purchased from a vendor called Bribertek. Dilbert raises his hand and asks whether the inflated prices are because the vendor offered the Boss a job. The Boss nervously insists it is only a coincidence.
punchline: Dilbert points out the obvious kickback, and sarcastically says that overpaying would be worthwhile if it got rid of the Boss, who flusters and denies any connection.
summary: A manager steers a hardware purchase to a suspiciously named vendor, and an employee calls out the apparent job-for-contract deal.

file: 2004/2004-05-16_celebrity business plan_commit crime_hire lawyer_reality tv show_gain weight_tabloids_spokesperson_weight loss product_write children book_rehab_addicted to painkillers_plan_future plans_goals_sensationalism.gif
title: Ratbert's Celebrity Career Plan

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Would you review my celebrity business plan?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: First, I'll commit a sensational crime that the media can't ignore.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Then I'll hire celebrity lawyer Johnny "Red" Galipigos to help me beat the rap.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'll use my fame to land a part on a reality TV show where I will win by cheating.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Then I'll gain a massive amount of weight so the tabloids will fixate on me.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Burp

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Then I'll become a spokesperson for a weight loss product.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: It works!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Lastly, I'll write children's books.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What about rehab?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Good catch. I totally forgot the part where I get addicted to painkillers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Otherwise, it looks good.

situation: Ratbert, standing on a stool, presents Dilbert with a step-by-step plan for becoming a celebrity: commit a crime, hire a famous lawyer, cheat on a reality show, gain weight, endorse a weight loss product, and write children's books. Dilbert, sitting in an armchair with a drink, only notices that the plan is missing the rehab stage.
punchline: Dilbert's only criticism is that Ratbert forgot the painkiller addiction and rehab step, implying that this scandal-ridden path is the standard formula for celebrity careers.
summary: A small white rat pitches a cynical blueprint for fame that mirrors every tabloid cliché, and his reviewer only wants the missing addiction chapter added.

title: Explaining Technology to Liberal Arts Majors

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Customer visit

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can see from your zombie stare that you don't understand technical talk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let me try it in a language I call "liberal arts major."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's blue.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It has a color??!

setting: Office meeting table during a customer visit
situation: Dilbert is meeting a customer and notices the customer's blank expression while he explains technical details. He offers to switch to a simplified 'liberal arts major' language and simply says the product is blue. The customer reacts with amazement that the product has a color.
punchline: Dilbert's dumbed-down explanation is so absurdly simple that the customer is astonished by the most trivial fact, while the strip also takes a swipe at liberal arts majors as being unable to grasp technology.
summary: After a customer glazes over at his technical pitch, an engineer tries a patronizingly basic description and still manages to wow him.

title: Ergophobia, a New Word for Laziness

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I got a bad case of ergophobia. It's an abnormal and persistent fear of work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Isn't everything about you a little abnormal and persistent?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yeah, but I'm still delighted when I discover new words for me.

setting: Office break area by the coffee maker
situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, tells Dilbert he has ergophobia, a fear of work. Dilbert, pouring coffee, remarks that everything about Wally is abnormal and persistent. Wally cheerfully agrees but says he still enjoys learning new labels for his own traits.
punchline: Wally treats his chronic work avoidance as a medical condition and happily collects fancy new words to describe himself, rather than doing anything about it.
summary: Wally proudly diagnoses himself with a technical-sounding fear of work, and shrugs off Dilbert's jab by saying he simply loves finding new names for his quirks.

file: 2004/2004-05-29_cut corners_bungling_budget process_skip design_testing and manufacturing_product recall_shipping_juggle.gif
title: Skipping Everything Except the Recall

transcript.speaker: Caption
transcript.text: Project meeting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll have to cut a few corners because of your bungling of the budget process.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If we skip design, prototype, testing and manufacturing, we can afford the product recall.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We'll save on shipping, too.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is bungle the same as juggle?

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: Dilbert tells his team he must cut corners because the boss botched the budget process. He then explains that by skipping design, prototyping, testing and manufacturing, they can afford the cost of a product recall. Alice adds sarcastically that they will save on shipping too, while the boss only wonders whether 'bungle' means 'juggle'.
punchline: Dilbert's budget-driven cuts eliminate every step of making a product, leaving only the recall, and the clueless boss misses the criticism entirely, fixating on the word 'bungle'.
summary: A budget-starved engineer sarcastically proposes dropping every stage of product development except the expensive recall, while his oblivious boss just wants a vocabulary lesson.

file: 2004/2004-12-06_problem_valuable advice_stare at screen_death_gather data_blinded by obvious_medical.gif
title: Blinded by the Obvious Advice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try working around the problem.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you for that valuable advice. I had planned to stare at my screen until I starved to death.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gather data before making a decision.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! I've been blinded by the obvious!

situation: The Boss stops by Dilbert's desk and offers a series of simple, self-evident tips for dealing with a problem. Dilbert sarcastically thanks him, then reacts with mock horror as the Boss adds yet another obvious platitude.
punchline: The Boss's "helpful" advice is so trivially obvious that Dilbert sarcastically claims it has blinded him, mocking managers who offer useless truisms as wisdom.
summary: A manager dispenses painfully obvious tips to an engineer, who answers with escalating sarcasm and theatrical despair.

file: 2004/2004-10-12_evil director_human resources_good news employee_trunover_scented kitty litter_downhill_quality_business.gif
title: Good News Means Not Burying Employees

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Good news about employee turnover...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm postponing my plan to bury poor performers in scented kitty litter.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Is it just me or has the quality of good news gone downhill?

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, announces at a meeting that he is delaying his plan to bury poor performers in scented kitty litter, presenting it as good news about employee turnover. Afterward a bald coworker and Dilbert stand with coffee, and the coworker remarks that good news has declined in quality.
punchline: The 'good news' is merely a temporary reprieve from a horrifying punishment, showing how low employees' expectations have sunk.
summary: An HR boss touts a delay in his gruesome plan for weak workers as cheerful news, leaving a colleague to lament how bad good news has become.

title: Catbert Confidentially Names Wally

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Can you tell me who complained about my off-color e-mail joke?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No, no, no.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: All conversations with human resources are strictly confidential.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, Wally, Wally, Wally, Wally, Wally, Wally...

situation: Carol asks Catbert, the HR director, who complained about her off-color e-mail joke. Catbert insists that HR conversations are strictly confidential. Then, high on a bag of catnip labeled super strength, he keeps babbling Wally's name, giving away the complainer.
punchline: Catbert's vow of confidentiality collapses the moment he gets into the catnip, and he compulsively blurts out Wally's name as the source of the complaint.
summary: An HR cat promises to protect a complainer's identity, then high on catnip he cannot stop repeating the name.

file: 2004/2004-11-15_product development_brain storm ideas_boredom_chocolate cake_after lunch_roast beef mittens.gif
title: Brainstorming Roast Beef Mittens

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Product development

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: First we'll cover the walls with brainstorm ideas.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How about something that turns boredom into chocolate cake?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I should have done this after lunch.

transcript.speaker: Unknown speaker (off-panel)
transcript.text: Roast beef mittens?

setting: Conference room during a product development brainstorming meeting
situation: The Boss opens a product development brainstorming session at a blank flip chart. Wally proposes an absurd product that turns boredom into chocolate cake, while Dilbert and Alice sit through it. A bored Boss thinks he should have scheduled the meeting after lunch, and someone off-panel suggests roast beef mittens.
punchline: Brainstorming produces ridiculous, food-obsessed ideas, and the Boss's thought that it would have been better after lunch suggests the meeting itself is as unproductive and unappetizing as the ideas.
summary: A product meeting begins with empty walls and quickly drifts into absurd snack-themed inventions while the Boss wishes he were eating.

title: Meeting Won't End Despite Hints

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll arrange my papers to signal that I want this meeting to end.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Tap tap tap

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: C'mon, take a hint!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Tap tap tap

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: So, as I was saying...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The man would not take a hint.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I said it's all gone!

setting: Office conference table, then a table with a coffee cup
situation: Dilbert sits in a meeting and taps his papers on the table, hoping his coworker will take the hint to end it. The coworker ignores the signal and keeps talking. In the last panel, Dilbert recounts the story to Dogbert, who is tipping an empty pitcher and says he already told a similar person it was all gone.
punchline: Subtle body-language hints don't work on oblivious people, so Dogbert's blunt statement that the coffee is all gone is the only thing that actually ends the conversation.
summary: A man shuffles his papers to politely end a meeting but his oblivious colleague keeps on talking, while Dogbert shows that bluntness is the only thing that works.

title: Pants-Optional Zone for Prima Donna

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a new prima donna. I already hate his guts, but he's indispensable.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He'll be dividing his time between being obnoxious and undermining my authority.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And the rules don't apply to him.

transcript.speaker: Prima Donna
transcript.text: I declare this a pants-optional zone.

situation: The Boss explains to his staff that he has hired a new prima donna employee he already dislikes but considers indispensable. punchline: The Boss's acknowledgement that the prima donna is exempt from the rules is instantly exploited when the new hire declares a ridiculous, inappropriate policy that the Boss is powerless to stop.
summary: A manager reluctantly introduces a star hire who is exempt from the rules, and the newcomer promptly abuses that freedom with an absurd decree.

title: Salary Spreadsheet Could Cause Riots

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'd have massive disloyalty, fights, vandalism, maybe even riots.

situation: The Boss tells Alice to send the salary spreadsheet to Human Resources and to keep everyone else from seeing it. He warns that employees learning what their coworkers earn would lead to disloyalty, fights, vandalism and even riots. Alice listens at her desk, and by the last panel she wears a wide, sinister grin.
punchline: The Boss's dire warning about riots implicitly admits that pay is distributed unfairly, and Alice's evil grin suggests she plans to leak the spreadsheet and start the chaos.
summary: A manager insists pay data must stay secret lest the workforce erupt, and his employee's malicious smile hints she may make that happen.

situation: Dogbert plays a TV stock analyst being interviewed on camera by a host at a desk. Asked whether he owns stock in the company he recommended, he admits he sold his shares immediately after his recommendation caused the price to spike. The host objects, and Dogbert cheerfully says he will use the profit to buy a helicopter.
punchline: The analyst openly admits to profiting from his own market-moving advice, shrugging off the ethical objection and gloating about a luxury purchase.
summary: A talk-show stock expert confesses to cashing out on his own hype and plans to spend the winnings on an aircraft.

situation: A troll across the desk from The Boss complains that every time the company cuts costs, its distributor Walgetco demands lower prices and keeps the savings. The Boss responds by reciting a retail store greeting as if he were a store employee. The troll suggests it may be too late, and The Boss cheerfully directs him to the troll accessories aisle.
punchline: The Boss has become so thoroughly a part of the big-box retailer's world that he treats a supplier's complaint about price pressure like a customer service interaction, implying the company is now just a powerless servant of Walgetco.
summary: A supplier grumbles about a retail giant squeezing its prices, and the boss answers with a store clerk's cheery script instead of any help.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, stands before the seated Boss and asks which project code he should bill his time to for a bizarre hypothetical. He describes someone's glasses falling into a urinal and the owner panicking and calling 911. He then admits it hasn't happened yet, but he can feel it coming.
punchline: Wally is pre-emptively seeking a billable project code for a ridiculous incident he's inventing and predicting, showing how he games time-tracking to avoid doing real work.
summary: Wally quizzes the Boss about where to bill his hours for a far-fetched toilet-related mishap that hasn't even occurred.

summary: Alice calmly turns a coworker's nitpicking about spelling mistakes back on the critic, exposing their own wasteful gossiping.

situation: The Boss opens a meeting by declaring quality the company's top priority. Alice and Dilbert keep asking whether quality outranks safety, legality and shareholder value, and each time the Boss concedes it does not. By the end he can only say quality is somewhere in the top four.
punchline: Every question knocks quality further down the list of priorities, showing that a 'top priority' is just empty rhetoric when it conflicts with safety, law and profit.
summary: A manager's claim that quality comes first collapses under a series of pointed questions until it ranks no higher than fourth.

situation: At a meeting, Dilbert gives his project status report by listing how many e-mails and voicemails the Boss has ignored. He adds that the Boss avoided him in the hallway by rambling about his sinus problems. The Boss starts to launch into the sinus topic again, and Wally, holding his coffee mug, eagerly says he wants to hear the stories.
punchline: Dilbert's complaint about the Boss's evasion becomes an opening for the Boss to start up his sinus stories again, while Wally, who normally avoids work, happily encourages a time-wasting tangent.
summary: A project status update turns into a complaint about an unresponsive manager who dodges communication with rambling health anecdotes, and the rambling promptly resumes.

punchline: Her disaster-magnet premonition is instantly proven right, as Wally's creepy thought shows the next romantic problem is already forming.
summary: A woman laments being a magnet for every kind of trouble, and right on cue a coworker in the room decides to make her his next stalking target.

title: Unclear Objectives Versus Boss's Effort

situation: Catbert, the HR director, reports to the Boss that employees' top complaint is unclear objectives. The Boss replies that his own top complaint is how much effort it takes to be clear. Catbert suggests calling it a tie, and the Boss asks why employees are so selfish.
punchline: The Boss treats his own laziness as an equal grievance to his employees' legitimate complaint, then blames them for being selfish for wanting clear direction.
summary: When told staff want clearer goals, a manager protests that giving clear goals is too much work for him and calls his workers selfish.

file: 2004/2004-03-07_boss's office_employee_exciting challenges_fertilized plant_hard work done_tree grows.gif

transcript.text: Good. Here's more work.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I don't understand.

transcript.text: Am I being punished for working hard?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, you're being rewarded with exciting new challenges.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Sproing!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Why does the plant grow faster when you say things like that?

transcript.text: No reason.

situation: An employee tells his boss he finished a project early by working nights and weekends, and the boss responds by handing him more work. When the employee asks if he is being punished, the boss claims it's a reward of exciting new challenges, and each of his insincere statements makes a potted plant grow bigger. By the end the plant has become a huge tree swallowing the office, and the boss keeps feeding it with more empty promises.
punchline: The boss's corporate platitudes are so full of manure that they literally fertilize the plant into a giant tree.
summary: A manager's bogus promises of rewards for hard work make his desk plant explode in size, since his words are plain fertilizer.
themes: rewarding hard work with more work

punchline: Dogbert wants a fake doctor title so that his usual insults get gratitude instead of resentment, mocking celebrity TV doctors who berate their audiences.
summary: Dogbert plans to rebrand himself as a television doctor so that the abuse he already hands out will be welcomed by his victims.

summary: Seeking the cheapest possible workforce, a boss tries to trap scruffy alley dwellers with dairy treats and a carrier.

summary: A lazy coworker proposes a date by insulting a frazzled colleague's life, betting that her bad decision-making will lead her to accept.

summary: A buyer who steered his company's business to a supplier expects an executive position in return, but the supplier's boss hides behind a waiting period.

file: 2004/2004-09-16_enormous brain_world changing_no pay_no cubilce_cling to ceiling_interviews well.gif

transcript.text: If you hire me, I will use my enormous brain to develop world-changing products.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I require no pay and no cubicle. I will eat used paper, and cling to the ceiling.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In my defense, he interviews very well.

setting: Interview room with a conference table
situation: A tall, bald-headed job candidate tells the Boss he will invent world-changing products, work for free, and live on the ceiling eating used paper. In the last panel Dilbert and the Boss sit beside the candidate, who has fallen asleep. The Boss defends hiring him by saying he interviews well.
punchline: The Boss has hired a bizarre, sleeping candidate and justifies it by claiming he does well in interviews, mocking how hiring decisions are based on interview performance rather than ability.
summary: A strange applicant promises genius and zero cost while acting like a creature, and the boss shrugs off the hire because of a good interview.

title: Buzzword Question After Three-Hour Meeting

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's been a great three-hour meeting but I have one question.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can a business-led project management process optimize our strategic core issues?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Was that gibberish?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I thought that's what we were doing.

situation: At the end of a three-hour meeting, a coworker praises it and then asks a question made up entirely of management buzzwords. The Boss, sitting at the table, asks whether the question was gibberish. The coworker replies that he thought gibberish was what everyone had been doing all along.
punchline: The meeting was so full of empty jargon that the coworker assumed speaking nonsense was the whole purpose of the discussion.
summary: After hours of corporate jargon, a meeting attendee poses a meaningless buzzword question and casually admits he believed nonsense was the point.

file: 2004/2004-05-11_non credible guy_invented reality tv_preposterous stories_picture hostility & curiosity_einstein_entertain realtives_new theory_liar_pathological liar_lies.gif
title: Humoring the Non-Credible Guy's Lies

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Non-Credible Guy

transcript.speaker: Non-Credible Guy
transcript.text: And that's how I invented "reality TV."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why don't you keep telling me preposterous stories while I stare at you with a mixture of hostility and curiosity?

transcript.speaker: Non-Credible Guy
transcript.text: And then Einstein asked me to entertain his relatives while he thought of a name for his new theory.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good, good.

situation: The Non-Credible Guy, a coworker labeled by a caption, boasts that he invented reality TV. Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, invites him to keep telling outrageous stories while Dilbert stares at him. The man continues with a story about entertaining Einstein's relatives, and Dilbert approves.
punchline: Dilbert, rather than challenging the obvious liar, explicitly asks for more absurd stories to be told while he watches with hostility and curiosity, treating the lies as entertainment.
summary: Instead of calling out a habitual fabricator, Dilbert gleefully prompts him to carry on spinning ridiculous tales for his own amusement.

title: Negotiator Spots Ordered Lie

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Negotiating

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been authorized to tell you that we have other offers.

transcript.speaker: Negotiator
transcript.text: I can tell from your phraseology that you've been ordered to lie and you're not good at it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What makes you think something like that?

transcript.speaker: Negotiator
transcript.text: There it is again!

setting: Conference room during a business negotiation
situation: Dilbert sits across a table from a counterpart in a negotiation and says he has been authorized to claim they have other offers. The counterpart cheerfully points out that Dilbert's wording shows he was ordered to lie and is bad at it. Dilbert nervously asks how they could tell, and the counterpart points at him, saying he just did it again.
punchline: Dilbert's awkward denial, asking what makes them think he's lying, is itself a clumsy tell that confirms he's an unskilled liar following orders.
summary: A reluctant negotiator is caught bluffing by his opponent, then gives himself away again while trying to deny it.

title: Reimbursing Company for Naughty Thoughts

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ethics Hotline

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is Dogbert. Please state your conundrum.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Sometimes I have naughty thoughts during work hours. Should I reimburse the company for lost productivity?

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Dang! This is costing me a fortune!

setting: Ethics hotline call center, and an office meeting table
situation: Dogbert answers a company ethics hotline, and a caller asks whether he owes the company money for time lost to naughty thoughts at work. In the final panel the same man sits grimacing at a meeting table next to an attractive woman, and his thought bubble reveals he is lamenting how much this is costing him.
punchline: The man is having naughty thoughts about the woman beside him in the very moment he worries about reimbursing the company, so his over-scrupulous honesty is racking up an ever-growing bill.
summary: A guilt-ridden employee phones an ethics line to ask if daydreaming about romance means he owes his employer money, then sits ogling a colleague while tallying the cost.

title: Shard-Filled Doughnuts for Pleasure-Seeking Morons

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My company is selling gigantic, shard-filled doughnuts with forty thousand calories apiece.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's based on Dogbert's theory that people are pleasure-seeking morons.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How does it taste?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Delicious! I have one for you strapped to my car.

setting: A kitchen or break area where a cook in a hairnet and apron stirs a pot
situation: Dilbert, holding a mug, explains to a hairnet-wearing cook that his company is selling enormous, glass-shard-filled doughnuts, a product built on Dogbert's theory about human nature. The cook asks how it tastes, and Dilbert, with his arm in a cast, cheerfully says it's delicious and that he has one strapped to his car for her.
punchline: Dilbert's injured arm and the doughnut strapped to his car show that the shard-filled product is dangerous, yet he enjoys it anyway, proving Dogbert's point that people are pleasure-seeking morons.
summary: A dangerous, absurdly caloric doughnut is marketed on the premise that consumers will chase pleasure regardless of harm, and even its injured fan keeps raving about it.

title: Death Spiral Budget Cut Methodology

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The leadership team can't decide where to make the deepest budget cuts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But don't worry. I offered to bring a systematic, data-driven focus to the process.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A death spiral goes clockwise north of the equator.

situation: At a conference table with Dilbert and a coworker, the Boss explains that leadership can't decide where to cut the budget, then says he offered to bring a systematic, data-driven approach. He then presents a flip chart where the budget cut areas (Research, Design, Sales, Marcom) form a circular loop, and explains it as a death spiral.
punchline: The Boss's 'systematic, data-driven' budget-cut method is just a circular chart of departments cutting each other in a death spiral, which he describes with meaningless pseudo-scientific trivia instead of any real analysis.
summary: A manager brags about applying rigorous analysis to layoffs, but his presentation is merely a looping diagram of departments chasing each other downward.

title: Liposuction Boss Keeps Eating Donuts

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How did the liposuction go?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: People say I look younger. And thanks to my self-discipline, I'll keep off the weight.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: One more.

setting: Conference room, then the boss's office
situation: In a meeting, Dilbert asks the boss how his liposuction went, and the boss brags that people say he looks younger and that his self-discipline will keep the weight off. In the last panel, the boss is slumped in an armchair while a subordinate feeds him donuts from a box, and he demands one more.
punchline: The boss boasts about his self-discipline while actually being hand-fed donuts, showing he has none and will regain the weight.
summary: A freshly slimmed boss praises his own willpower right before an employee is shown feeding him box after box of donuts.
